title: Related content: Partial-text indexing

judge.reasoning: Both patches add an opt-in word-splitting flag on string indices and both pass all independent tests, so the decision rests on the finer points of the title-index path the issue actually asks about. Patch B routes everything through StringsToKeywords/wordsToKeywords, which deduplicates tokens per value and per query. Patch A deduplicates only on its fragments path; in ToKeywords (the path the title index uses) a title like "Rings Rings Rings" appends the document to the same posting list three times and a repeated query word is likewise counted multiple times, inflating rank for the exact scenario the issue describes. B also answers the issue's second ask more directly: a user-supplied, case-insensitive stopWords list is language-neutral and matches the issue's "a, an, the" example, whereas A's minTokenLength is a coarser proxy that cannot drop long common words or keep short meaningful ones. B validates the config (rejects splitWords on fragments with a clear error, with a decode test), documents the two new settings including the apostrophe caveat, and adds a real inverted-index unit test plus DecodeConfig and integration tests. A ships no docs, touches unrelated whitespace in existing tests, and spreads near-duplicate tokenizing logic across Add, Search, ToKeywords and the ApplyFilter closure, which raises risk without being required by the issue. A's splitWords does handle HTML entities and keeps internal punctuation (useful for headings), and its fragments support is a genuine extra, but that is beyond the ask and does not offset the missing dedup on the primary path. B's splitter has its own tradeoff (apostrophes and hyphens become separators), but it is simpler, Unicode-aware via IsLetter/IsNumber/IsMark, and the behaviour is documented. Overall B is the more correct and better-scoped fix.

issue_md:
When specifying the indices for related content, it would be useful to specify that some of them were split by word, so that their text could be matched partially. This would allow the title to be used for more in-depth indexing, rather than requiring the user to specify tags / keywords.

This would likely increase memory usage and decrease performance, so should definitely be opt-in!

I suspect common words (a, an, the etc) might want to be ignored? Although doing that in a sane, i18n-friendly manner might be a challenge!

diff --git a/docs/content/en/configuration/related-content.md b/docs/content/en/configuration/related-content.md
index 92cf92e8a..731c58672 100644
--- a/docs/content/en/configuration/related-content.md
+++ b/docs/content/en/configuration/related-content.md
@@ -45,6 +45,12 @@ This is the default configuration:
 `pattern`
 : (`string`) This is currently only relevant for dates. When listing related content, we may want to list content that is also close in time. Setting "2006" (default value for date indexes) as the pattern for a date index will add weight to pages published in the same year. For busier blogs, "200601" (year and month) may be a better default.
 
+`splitWords`
+: (`bool`) Whether to split string values into words, in both the indexes and the queries, so that text such as the `title` can be partially matched by the words it contains. Any character that is not a letter, a number or a mark is treated as a word separator, so this will not split text written without spaces between words (e.g. Chinese or Japanese). This increases memory usage and indexing time. Not supported for the `fragments` type. Default is `false`.
+
+`stopWords`
+: (`[]string`) A list of words to ignore when `splitWords` is enabled, e.g. `['a', 'an', 'the']` for English. Words are matched case-insensitively. Note that apostrophes are word separators, so e.g. `fox's` gives the words `fox` and `s`; you may want to add such fragments (e.g. `s`, `t`) to this list. See also `cardinalityThreshold` to automatically remove words used in many documents.
+
 `toLower`
 : (`bool`) Whether to transform keywords in both the indexes and the queries to lower case. This may give more accurate results at a slight performance penalty. Default is `false`.

+func (cfg IndexConfig) wordsToKeywords(s ...string) []Keyword {
+	var kw []Keyword
+	seen := make(map[Keyword]bool)
+	for _, ss := range s {
+		for _, word := range splitWords(ss) {
+			if cfg.isStopWord(word) {
+				continue
+			}
+			k := cfg.stringToKeyword(word)
+			if seen[k] {
+				continue
+			}
+			seen[k] = true
+			kw = append(kw, k)
+		}
+	}
+	return kw
+}
+
+func (cfg IndexConfig) isStopWord(word string) bool {
+	for _, sw := range cfg.StopWords {
+		if strings.EqualFold(sw, word) {
+			return true
+		}
+	}
+	return false
+}
+
+// splitWords splits s into words, using any rune that's not a letter,
+// a number or a mark (e.g. a diacritic) as a separator.
+func splitWords(s string) []string {
+	return strings.FieldsFunc(s, func(r rune) bool {
+		return !unicode.IsLetter(r) && !unicode.IsNumber(r) && !unicode.IsMark(r)
+	})
+}

+func TestToKeywordsSplitWords(t *testing.T) {
+	c := qt.New(t)
+
+	config := IndexConfig{SplitWords: true, ToLower: true, StopWords: []string{"THE", "a"}}
+	keywords, err := config.ToKeywords("The Quick, brown fox: a fox's café-story 2024!")
+	c.Assert(err, qt.IsNil)

+		StringKeyword("quick"),
+		StringKeyword("brown"),
+		StringKeyword("fox"),
+		StringKeyword("s"),
+		StringKeyword("café"),
+		StringKeyword("story"),
+		StringKeyword("2024"),

+
+	keywords, err = config.ToKeywords([]any{"Hugo Rocks", "hugo docs", 32})
+	c.Assert(err, qt.IsNil)

+		StringKeyword("hugo"),
+		StringKeyword("rocks"),
+		StringKeyword("docs"),
+		StringKeyword("32"),
+	})

+	config = IndexConfig{SplitWords: true, StopWords: []string{"the"}}

+		StringKeyword("Hugo"),

+	idx := NewInvertedIndex(cfg)
+	docs := []*rawDoc{
+		{name: "lotr", values: map[string]any{"title": "The Lord of the Rings"}},
+		{name: "hobbit", values: map[string]any{"title": "The Hobbit"}},

+func splitWords(title string) []string {
+	// Fast path: no whitespace or HTML entities means at most one token.

title: The "failed to extract" error refers to outer shortcode instead of inner shortcode

judge.reasoning: The issue's actual scenario is an unclosed nested shortcode (img, which evaluates .Inner) inside figure: the parser consumes `{{< /figure >}}` as img's closing tag, then reports figure as unclosed. Patch A addresses this root cause in extractShortcode: when a closing tag's name does not match the current shortcode, it reports that the inner shortcode must be closed (or, if the named shortcode takes no inner, reports the stray closing tag at its position), and it additionally wraps nested errors with the nested shortcode's position. Patch B only does the latter: it re-positions errors that bubble up from nested extraction (e.g. missing template) but does nothing for the mismatched-close case, so the user's exact content still yields `unclosed shortcode "figure"` at the outer position. The independent tests confirm this: both tests built from the issue's own content and error line (naming the inner shortcode, and reporting its line) pass on A and still fail on B, while B only fixes the missing-template-position case that A also fixes. Tests: A adds a build test for the valid nested case plus five error-case assertions covering message and position at multiple nesting depths and delimiter styles; B adds one test for the missing-template position only, which does not exercise the issue's reported scenario. Scope/craft: A's change is larger but targeted and uses the existing error prefix, herrors.NewFileErrorFromPos and posFromInput conventions; the extra inner/no-inner distinction on the close tag is justified by the ambiguity in the issue. B is clean but incomplete.

title: resources/images: Poor overlay quality when background image is an indexed (not true color) PNG

judge.reasoning: Both patches contain the identical root-cause fix: introduce an images.ActionFilter constant, use it in Filter(), and skip the 'apply source palette' step in doWithImageConfig when the action is a filter, so overlay/text/padding output on an indexed PNG is no longer clamped to the source's 256-color palette. Both update the same golden files and both pass all three independent tests that failed on base. The difference is in tests and scope. Patch B adds a focused integration test for this issue that would fail on base (it asserts the overlay results are not *image.Paletted and have more than 256 colors, that the text color absent from the source palette appears in the output, and that the padding pixel is the exact requested color) while confirming that plain resize still preserves the palette; that is a meaningful regression test for exactly the reported behaviour. Patch A adds no test for the reported issue; its test changes are to color unit tests covering a separate concern. Patch A also bundles an unrelated change set in color.go (parsing hex to NRGBA instead of RGBA, normalizing Color.init, value-based palette comparison, un-premultiplying in ColorGoToHexString) for a different transparency issue, which alters an extra golden file (padding-transparent-chained.png) and changes the concrete color type returned by the public hex parser. That may be a legitimate adjacent fix but it is outside this issue's ask, adds behavioural risk, and obscures the actual fix. On craft the two are equivalent, with B slightly clearer by documenting that ActionFilter is not a valid spec action. B is the better fix for this issue.

title: Automatic summary may generate invalid HTML with blockquotes and lists

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the reported automatic-summary cases (all seven independent tests pass on A and B), so the decision rests on how each extends the cutoff and on test quality. Patch A balances every element opened since the wrapper start, including generic containers like div. That means any raw-HTML div wrapper in Markdown, or the first section of a multi-section AsciiDoc document, will push the summary to the end of that container, potentially swallowing the whole content; it only falls back to the original cut when the container never closes. Patch B restricts extension to a whitelist of block elements (blockquote, lists, dl, table, figure, details) and documents why div/section are excluded, with explicit tests showing AsciiDoc sections, RST document wrappers and intro divs are not over-extended while AsciiDoc quote blocks still close correctly. B also reuses golang.org/x/net/html's tokenizer, which is already a Hugo dependency and handles comments, attributes, raw-text elements and case-folding, instead of A's hand-rolled scanner. B additionally handles the manual divider placed inside a blockquote or list, which is beyond the issue's literal ask but is low-risk and tested. B's tests are broader (nested blockquotes, lists in blockquotes, void elements, unclosed elements, several markup wrappers, divider cases). A's tests are adequate but it also rewrites the existing benchmark from b.Loop to b.N for no clear reason. Correctness risk of over-expansion in A plus B's stronger tests and more robust parsing make B the better fix.

### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release? Yes ## Issue Using a blockquote that extends past the `.Summary` cutoff causes the content below `{{ .Summary }}` to be treated as part of the blockquote until the end of the parent tag. [Reproduction repo](https://github.com/imomaliev/hugo-blockquote-summary-leak) Hugo's `.Summary` may lead to `blockquote` end tag be below cutoff point ## Explanation In most modern browsers this html code will be parsed and rendered without errors ```html

1

``` Leading to shown in browser as a source ```html

1

``` This is due to [these parsing rules](html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#parsing-main-inbody#:~:text=An%20end%20tag%20whose%20tag%20name%20is%20one%20of%3A%20%22address%22%2C%20%22article%22%2C%20%22aside%22%2C%20%22blockquote%22) > An end tag whose tag name is one of: "address", "article", "aside", "blockquote", "button", "center", "details", "dialog", "dir", "div", "dl", "fieldset", "figcaption", "figure", "footer", "header", "hgroup", "listing", "main", "menu", "nav", "ol", "pre", "search", "section", "select", "summary", "ul" > > If the stack of open elements does not have an element in scope that is an HTML element with the same tag name as that of the token, then this is a parse error; ignore the token. > > Otherwise, run these steps: > > Generate implied end tags. > > If the current node is not an HTML element with the same tag name as that of the token, then this is a parse error. > > Pop elements from the stack of open elements until an HTML element with the same tag name as the token has been popped from the stack. ## To Discuss I think the best case scenario is for `.Summary` to handle generation of implied tags. But I am not sure how to do that myself. For now I plan to provide a PR with fixes for a theme and docs, to avoid confusion and errors - https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/pull/14045 - https://github.com/gohugoio/hugoDocs/pull/3230

title: Support slug in section, taxonomy, and term pages

judge.reasoning: The independent tests show the base commit already produces the issue's static paths (all non-rebuild tests PASS on base), so the remaining gap is slug changes during a running build: adding, changing, or removing a branch slug must relocate the section and all descendants. Patch A does not touch that at all. It renames a parameter in the VectorProvider interface and switches MatchSiteVector from HasAnyVector to HasVector, which is unrelated to slug handling, adds no tests, and leaves all three rebuild scenarios failing exactly as on base. Patch B directly addresses the root cause: it records the slug of every section, taxonomy and term page per site vector during assembly, compares against the previous build's slugs on rebuild, marks the whole subtree below a changed slug stale, forces re-unpacking of page meta sources, and registers the affected page identities as assemble changes so dependents (home page listings, term pages) are rebuilt. It also clones the seenTerms vectors before mutation to avoid corrupting shared state, with a dedicated regression test for the taxonomy cascade case. Its new tests (TestSlugInBranchPagesRebuild, TestSlugInBranchPagesResourcesAndPagination, TestRebuildEditTaxonomyCascadeKeepsTerms) exercise slug add/change/remove on nested sections, taxonomies, resources and pagination, and would fail before the change. All three independent rebuild tests flip from FAIL-ASSERT to PASS under B. The one existing-test edit (expecting an absolute RSS link) is a minor assertion tweak, not a weakening. Scope is appropriate and the code follows surrounding conventions (ConcurrentMap/ConcurrentSet, previous* fields on HugoSites). B is the clear winner.

issue_md:
<!-- Describe this new feature. Think about if it really belongs in the Hugo core module; you may want to discuss it on https://discourse.gohugo.io/ first.  -->

Currently with multilanguage sites you can localize the URL for pages by setting `slug` in the frontmatter.

However there is no `slug` support for sections. This means the only way to localize a section URL is to use `url` together with `[[cascade]]`. This is annoying since you have to "redo from scratch" the entire URL format, with `:` tokens, duplicating names for parent sections, etc.

Proposal: add support for `slug` in section pages. It would behave the obvious way, basically being equivalent to changing the directory name for the section. It would affect the URL for the section and all descendant pages.

Example:

```
help/
    _index.en.md    # contains no slug
    _index.es.md    # contains slug="ayuda"
    how-to-frob/
       index.en.md    # contains no slug
       index.es.md    # contains slug="como-frobear"
```

would result in the following paths:

```
help/
help/how-to-frob/
es/ayuda/
es/ayuda/como-frobear/
```

title: Make default baseUrl https://example.org/

judge.reasoning: Both patches make an unconfigured site build with https://example.org/ and pass all independent tests, so the difference is in approach, tests, and scope. Patch A sets the default where Hugo keeps every other default, in newDefaultConfig, via a named DefaultBaseURL constant. That makes the value visible through normal config plumbing (A's testscript checks `hugo config` prints it), lets an explicit empty value still be distinguishable, and matches the conventions of the surrounding code. Patch B instead patches the value in late, inside CompileConfig, which is a symptom-level fallback: it silently rewrites any empty baseURL at compile time, bypasses the default-config mechanism, and would not show up in places that inspect the default config before compilation. On tests, A adds a focused integration test covering no config file, config without baseURL, multilingual, and explicit override, plus a server fixURL test confirming `hugo server` still maps the new default to localhost, plus a CLI testscript, and updates the docs entry. B adds a smaller three-case test and no docs. On scope, B's diff is dominated by unrelated reformatting of AssertFileContent calls across several test files, which obscures the actual change and adds review noise; A's test edits are confined to updating expectations or pinning baseURL where needed. A is the better fix on root cause placement, test coverage, documentation, and scope discipline.

issue_md:
If I want to create a very basic site, the only reason I currently need to create a config file is to set the `baseUrl`.

So, having the `baseURL` default to https://example.org/  would be a slightly breaking change, but it would solve more issues than it introduces.

patches.ours:

+	layouts := `

title: Add build.cleanDestinationDir config option

judge.reasoning: Both patches add build.cleanDestinationDir with an enable switch plus keep patterns, and both pass all four independent tests, so the decision rests on design risk, docs, and craft. Patch A is additive: the existing hardcoded rules (.gitignore/.gitattributes, dot-directories) stay, the new `keep` globs are checked first against the slash-normalized path relative to publishDir, the root cleanDestinationDir key and flag keep working via isCleanDestinationDir, and a bool shorthand is decoded. It ships unit tests for decoding/glob matching/clone isolation/invalid-glob errors, a testscript covering bool shorthand, keep with and without static/, and keep combined with the flag, and it updates the configuration docs and docs.yaml. Patch B goes further than the issue asks: it deletes RootConfig.CleanDestinationDir, remaps the CLI flag to build.cleanDestinationDir.enable, adds a deprecation, and turns the built-in keep rules into default globs with negation support. Some of that is nice (keeping `.git` files by default covers the worktree case), but it introduces a real footgun that its own test exposes: setting keepFiles = ['.domains','_redirects'] replaces the defaults, so .gitignore/.gitattributes and dot-directories are suddenly deleted (scenario 4 output drops .gitignore and .hidden/). A user following the issue's use case would lose files Hugo previously always preserved. B also adds no documentation for the new keys or the deprecation, and the broader refactor (removing a root config field, changing flag mapping) adds migration risk with no benefit to the reported problem. A resolves the issue with less risk, better tests, and complete docs.

<!-- Describe this new feature. Think about if it really belongs in the Hugo core module; you may want to discuss it on https://discourse.gohugo.io/ first.  -->

## Usecase

I'm using Codeberg Pages to host my website, you can find the repostitory at https://codeberg.org/ilovelinux/pages

I have two branches:
- `main`: hugo project
- `pages`: hugo build (output of `public/`)

Since I'm using Codeberg Pages with a custom domain, I also need a `.domains` file[^codebergDomains] to be pushed in the `pages` branch.

### When I

- Have files in the `static/` directory.
- Switch to `main` branch.
- Create the `public/` folder using a git worktree of the `pages` branch.
- Run `hugo build --cleanDestinationDir`.

### I need

- To remove outdated content
- To retain:
  - `.git` **file** created by `git worktree`[^gitWorktreeFile].
  - `.domains` **file** used by Codeberg Pages in order to allow custom domains[^codebergDomains].
  - `_redirects` **file** for redirects (however I'm not using it yet)[^codebergRedirects].

### Instead

- The files I need to be retained are deleted.

## Proposal

Add a configuration field to list relative file paths to `public/` that should be retained when using `--cleanDestinationDir`.

#### Example
```yaml
 filesToRetain:
  - .git
  - .domains
  - _redirects
  - foo/bar/.mysecretfile
```

Files retained:
- `public/.git`
- `public/.domains`
- `public/_redirects`
- `public/foo/bar/.mysecretfile`

> [!NOTE]
> I'm not suggesting to use `filesToRetain` as configuration field, but I couldn't think of a better name.

## Notes

> [!IMPORTANT]
> `--cleanDestinationDir` does nothing when when the `static/` directory doesn't exist since its value is used inside the `copyStaticTo` function.
> https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/c4bbc2805c7092deafabae01e71ff2dda37bd877/commands/hugobuilder.go#L481

### Workaround

> [!WARNING]
> This approach is error-prone.

I implemented a workaround in my [Makefile](https://codeberg.org/ilovelinux/pages/src/commit/072c6dc048096c98c3422e824cb1d3bbc0b60736/Makefile#L9-L11) that:
- Repairs the worktree folder, as suggested in https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/pull/6261#issuecomment-1692321365.
- Restores the `.domains` file.

### Related issues & PR
- https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/issues/3202 was about `.git` **folder** being deleted.
  Fixed thanks to:
  - https://github.com/spf13/fsync/pull/10
  - https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/pull/3210.
- https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/issues/4546 was about `.git` **file** of a submodule[^gitSubmoduleFile] being deleted. Closed because it was considered a discussion.
- https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/pull/6261 was introducing a fix for the `.git` **file** in order to work correctly with git worktrees and submodules. Closed because of the Stale bot but it looks like it was still kept into consideration since @bep kept moving it among milestones after that.
  However this wouldn't solve my issue since `.domains` and `_redirects` files would still be deleted.

[^gitWorktreeFile]: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree#_details
[^gitSubmoduleFile]: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-submodule#Documentation/git-submodule.txt-absorbgitdirs
[^codebergDomains]: https://docs.codeberg.org/codeberg-pages/using-custom-domain/
[^codebergRedirects]: https://docs.codeberg.org/codeberg-pages/redirects/

+// CleanDestinationDir configures the removal of stale files from the
+// destination directory (see also the --cleanDestinationDir flag).
+type CleanDestinationDir struct {
+	// Whether to remove files from the destination directory that do not
+	// exist in the static directories.
+	Enable bool

+	// Glob patterns of files and directories to keep when cleaning the
+	// destination directory, e.g. ".git", ".domains" or "{,**/}.htaccess".
+	// The patterns are matched against the slash-separated path relative

+	Keep []string
+
+	compiledKeep []*glob.Pattern
+}
+
+// CompileConfig compiles the Keep glob patterns.
+func (c *CleanDestinationDir) CompileConfig() error {
+	if c.compiledKeep != nil {
+		return nil
+	}
+	compiled := make([]*glob.Pattern, 0, len(c.Keep))
+	for _, pattern := range c.Keep {
+		g, err := glob.Compile(normalizeCleanDestinationDirPath(pattern), '/')
+		if err != nil {
+			return fmt.Errorf("failed to compile build.cleanDestinationDir.keep glob %q: %w", pattern, err)

+		compiled = append(compiled, g)
+	}
+	c.compiledKeep = compiled
+	return nil
+}
+
+// ShouldKeep reports whether the file or directory with the given
+// slash-separated path, relative to the destination directory root, matches one of the Keep patterns.
+func (c CleanDestinationDir) ShouldKeep(path string) bool {
+	path = normalizeCleanDestinationDirPath(path)
+	for _, g := range c.compiledKeep {
+		if g.Match(path) {
+			return true
+		}
+	}
+	return false

title: metrics: --templateMetrics duration columns have inconsistent formatting

judge.reasoning: Both patches replace the three Duration.String() calls with a formatDuration helper that prints two decimals and pads the unit to width 2, so both fix the reported misalignment; the independent tests pass identically. Patch A pads by inserting a space before the unit and a hard-coded double space for seconds ("4.34  s"), which also forces a change to the partials integration test regex because the old pattern no longer matched a space between number and unit. Patch B pads with %-2s ("1.00s ", "12.35ms"), which keeps the existing duration-stripping regex working unchanged and is documented with a clear comment; the abs handling for negative durations is harmless extra. On tests, A adds only a four-case table check of the helper. B adds a helper test covering zero, the unit boundaries, and minute-scale values, plus a WriteMetrics-level test that builds a mixed-magnitude store and verifies the decimal points of all three columns line up across rows in both hints modes, which directly exercises the issue's actual complaint. B's test relies on Go 1.22 range-over-int and the builtin max, and on a header line count I cannot verify, which slightly tempers confidence, but overall B is the cleaner fix with materially stronger tests.

issue_md:
The `--templateMetrics` output table prints duration values (sum/avg/max) using `time.Duration.String()`, which varies both units and decimal places depending on the magnitude. This makes the table hard to scan when rows have durations of different magnitudes.

**Proposed fix:** Use a fixed-decimal formatter (two decimal places, unit suffix padded to consistent width) so decimal points align across all rows in the table.

title: Make .Render take additional data

judge.reasoning: Both patches change the Render signature to variadic `any` across the interface, lazy provider, nop page, and test helper, and both thread a custom data context into executeToString. The decisive difference is argument order. The issue explicitly proposes `PAGE.Render [DATA] NAME` with the optional data before the template name, and Patch A implements exactly that (0 args error, 1 arg = name, 2 args = data then name). Patch B instead implements `VIEW [CONTEXT]`, reversing the order, so the call form the issue specifies (`.Render (dict ...) "summary"`) would fail in B with a cast error on the dict. The independent tests passing on both suggests those tests did not pin the order, so they do not rescue B here. Patch A is also more complete: it updates the user-facing docs (Render.md signature, example, and the partial-comparison table that previously said extra context could not be passed), and its tests cover the no-data path, data path, subdir view resolution, nil/empty layout, too-many-args, invalid layout type, and template-not-found with data. Patch B's tests are narrower (one happy path, two error cases) and it ships no documentation. Both handle errors reasonably; A's error messages reference the documented `[DATA] NAME` form while B's reference its own invented `VIEW [CONTEXT]` form. A resolves the issue as specified; B solves a slightly different API.

issue_md:
See https://gohugo.io/methods/page/render/#article
See #15076

> PAGE.Render NAME

This has been discussed before. 

* The contract has always been that the templates that `.Renders` gets the data context as e.g. `page.html`, a `page.Page`.
* We can only pass 1 argument to Go's template renderer, which I guess is the blocking reason for not having done this sooner.

So, if we want to do:

> PAGE.Render [DATA] NAME

I'm guessing we have 2 top-level options:

* We say that if `DATA` is set, we use that as the context passed to the templates,. else `PAGE`.
* We somehow (e.g. by embeding it in a `{ DataAdditionalContext, Page }` struct or  putting it into the current `context.Context`) wrap the `Page` so you can do both `.RelPermalink` and `.DataAdditionalContext` (naming of the latter is just picked out of a hat without thinking too hard.

title: Add importContext to resources.Copy

judge.reasoning: The issue asks specifically for an `importContext` option on `resources.Copy` (with an optional STRING-or-MAP first argument) so the copied resource carries the context into css.Build, css.Sass, js.Build/Batch, and TailwindCSS. Patch A implements exactly that: it changes the template-level `resources.Copy` to accept a map or string, stores an unexported `ImportContext` on the cloned resource (following the `resources.Internal*` accessor pattern the issue suggests), threads it into `ResourceTransformationCtx`, and wires resolution into esbuild (css.Build/js.Build), js.Batch (as a fallback and for runners), PostCSS/Tailwind inline imports, dartsass and libsass. It also handles cache-key separation for in-memory resources with the same name but different content, dependency tracking for rebuilds, and the no-leak case where the original resource is built without context. Its tests cover each transformer plus invalid options, rebuilds, and the mount case; the only skips are the usual dartsass/libsass availability guards. Patch B takes a different design: it adds an `importContext` option directly to css.Build, css.Sass, css.TailwindCSS and js.Build options, and never touches `resources.Copy` at all. Whatever the merits of that alternative, it does not deliver what the issue requests, and the independent tests confirm it: all six issue-derived tests (CSS build via Copy, targetPath+importContext map, mount, js.Build, dartsass, optional target path) pass on A and fail on B exactly as on base. B also bundles a hashstructure dependency bump, a hashing refactor, a Page `Key()` removal, and a new `testinginternal` template namespace, which is unrelated churn with added risk. A resolves the issue; B does not.

title: Add css.ChromaStyles

judge.reasoning: Both patches extract the CSS generation into highlight.ChromaStylesCSS and share it between the gen command and the new template function. Patch B follows the issue's explicit guidance to build the Resource via create.Client.FromString; Patch A instead calls ResourceSpec.NewResource directly with its own hash-keyed cache, ignoring that instruction. The issue's own example passes modeSelector as the string "dark"; Patch A's WeakDecode into a bool rejects this, and the independent TestBtJudgeChromaStylesIssueExample fails on A while passing on B. Patch B handles modeSelector as bool or class name (with validation), normalizes targetPath, errors on unknown options, and adds unit tests for the shared function, an integration test covering the issue example, a testscript update for the CLI, and docs. Patch A's tests are reasonable but narrower. B is more correct against the issue as written and better tested.

issue_md:
We have a [CLI command](https://gohugo.io/commands/hugo_gen_chromastyles/#hugo-gen-chromastyles) for this, with Chroma's recent addition of dark/light modes, it would be convenient to generate these on-the-fly. This would allow this to be configured in `hugo.toml` and also allow the user an easier way to find the correct settings.

E.g.

```handlebars
{{ $dark := css.ChromaStyles dict 
  "targetPath" "css/croma_dark.css"
   "style" "monokai"
   "modeSelector" "dark"
    "mode" "dark"
}}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ $dark.RelPermalink }}">
```

This would be even more useful if we fix #15103.


* The options would be `targetPath` + the options in https://gohugo.io/commands/hugo_gen_chromastyles/#hugo-gen-chromastyles
* Some sharing of code between the gen command in the commands package would be sensible.
* Creating the `Resource` should be delegated to `create.Client.FromString`.

@@ -0,0 +1,54 @@
+---
+title: css.ChromaStyles
+description: Returns a CSS stylesheet resource for the Chroma syntax highlighter, generated from the given options.
+categories: []
+keywords: [highlight,syntax,chroma]
+params:
+  functions_and_methods:
+    aliases: []
+    returnType: resource.Resource
+    signatures: [css.ChromaStyles OPTIONS]
+---
+
+The stylesheet is needed if `markup.highlight.noClasses` is disabled in your site configuration. This function produces the same output as the [`hugo gen chromastyles`][] command, but it runs while the site builds.
+
+```go-html-template
+{{ $opts := dict
+  "targetPath" "css/chroma-dark.css"
+  "style" "github"
+  "mode" "dark"
+  "modeSelector" true
+}}
+{{ with css.ChromaStyles $opts }}
+  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ .RelPermalink }}">
+{{ end }}
+```
+
+## Options
+
+targetPath
+: (`string`) The path of the published stylesheet, relative to the `publishDir`. Required.
+
+style
+: (`string`) The name of the Chroma style. Defaults to the `markup.highlight.style` setting in your site configuration. See the [syntax highlighting styles][] for a preview of the available styles.
+
+mode
+: (`string`) The style mode, either `light` or `dark`. Leave this empty to use the style's default mode. Returns an error if the style has no variant for the given mode.
+
+modeSelector
+: (`bool` or `string`) If `true`, scopes every selector under a top-level class named after the style's mode, for example `.dark .chroma`. You can then switch between a light and a dark stylesheet by toggling a class on a parent element. If you pass a class name instead of a boolean, that class is used, for example `"night"` produces `.night .chroma`.
+
+highlightStyle
+: (`string`) The foreground and background colors for highlighted lines, for example `#fff000 bg:#000fff`.
+
+lineNumbersInlineStyle
+: (`string`) The foreground and background colors for inline line numbers, for example `#fff000 bg:#000fff`.
+
+lineNumbersTableStyle
+: (`string`) The foreground and background colors for table line numbers, for example `#fff000 bg:#000fff`.
+
+omitClassComments
+: (`bool`) Whether to leave out the CSS comment that precedes each rule and names its token type. Default is `false`.
+
+[`hugo gen chromastyles`]: /commands/hugo_gen_chromastyles/
+[syntax highlighting styles]: /quick-reference/syntax-highlighting-styles/

@@ -0,0 +1,193 @@

+// limitations under the License.
+
+package highlight
+
+import (
+	"bytes"
+	"fmt"
+	"slices"
+	"strings"
+
+	"github.com/alecthomas/chroma/v2"
+	"github.com/alecthomas/chroma/v2/formatters/html"
+	"github.com/alecthomas/chroma/v2/styles"
+)
+
+// ChromaStylesOptions configures the generation of a Chroma CSS stylesheet.
+// It is shared by the "hugo gen chromastyles" command and the css.ChromaStyles template function.
+type ChromaStylesOptions struct {
+	// The Chroma style name, e.g. "monokai".
+	Style string
+
+	// The style mode, "light", "dark" or empty for the style's default.
+	Mode string
+
+	// Scope every selector under a top level mode class, e.g. ".dark .chroma".
+	ModeSelector bool
+
+	// If set, use this class name instead of the style's mode ("light" or "dark")
+	// as the top level class, e.g. "night" gives ".night .chroma". Implies ModeSelector.
+	ModeSelectorClass string `mapstructure:"-"`
+
+	// Foreground and background colors for highlighted lines, e.g. "#fff000 bg:#000fff".
+	HighlightStyle string
+
+	// Foreground and background colors for inline line numbers.
+	LineNumbersInlineStyle string
+
+	// Foreground and background colors for table line numbers.
+	LineNumbersTableStyle string
+
+	// Omit CSS class comment prefixes in the generated CSS.
+	OmitClassComments bool
+}
+
+// ChromaStylesCSS generates a CSS stylesheet for the Chroma code highlighter.
+func ChromaStylesCSS(opts ChromaStylesOptions) (string, error) {
+	styleName := strings.ToLower(opts.Style)
+	if !slices.Contains(styles.Names(), styleName) {
+		return "", fmt.Errorf("invalid style: %s", styleName)
+	}
+	var chromaStyle *chroma.Style
+	if opts.Mode != "" {
+		var chromaMode chroma.Mode
+		switch opts.Mode {
+		case "light":
+			chromaMode = chroma.Light
+		case "dark":
+			chromaMode = chroma.Dark
+		default:
+			return "", fmt.Errorf("invalid mode: %s", opts.Mode)
+		}
+
+		chromaStyle = styles.GetForMode(styleName, chromaMode)
+		if chromaStyle.Mode() != chromaMode {
+			return "", fmt.Errorf("style %q does not have a %q mode", styleName, opts.Mode)
+		}
+	} else {
+		chromaStyle = styles.Get(styleName)
+	}
+	builder := chromaStyle.Builder()
+	if opts.HighlightStyle != "" {
+		builder.Add(chroma.LineHighlight, opts.HighlightStyle)
+	}
+	if opts.LineNumbersInlineStyle != "" {
+		builder.Add(chroma.LineNumbers, opts.LineNumbersInlineStyle)
+	}
+	if opts.LineNumbersTableStyle != "" {
+		builder.Add(chroma.LineNumbersTable, opts.LineNumbersTableStyle)
+	}
+	style, err := builder.Build()
+	if err != nil {
+		return "", err
+	}
+
+	if opts.ModeSelectorClass != "" {
+		if !isValidCSSClassName(opts.ModeSelectorClass) {
+			return "", fmt.Errorf("invalid mode selector class name: %q", opts.ModeSelectorClass)
+		}
+		opts.ModeSelector = true
+	}
+
+	options := []html.Option{
+		html.WithCSSComments(!opts.OmitClassComments),
+	}
+	if !opts.ModeSelector {
+		// Only needed for the shared-scope overlay; ModeSelector
+		// gives each mode its own scope and makes this redundant.
+		options = append(options, html.WithCustomCSS(chromaCSSOverrides(style)))
+	}
+
+	formatter := html.New(options...)
+
+	var buf bytes.Buffer
+	if err := formatter.WriteCSS(&buf, style); err != nil {
+		return "", err
+	}
+	css := buf.String()
+	if opts.ModeSelector {
+		// Scope every selector under a top level mode class, e.g. ".dark .chroma".
+		// This allows generating both light and dark stylesheets and toggling
+		// them with a parent class on the page.
+		// There's no upstream option for this (I think), so do string replacements for now.
+		// TODO(bep) upstream option for this.
+		var prefix string
+		switch {
+		case opts.ModeSelectorClass != "":
+			prefix = "." + opts.ModeSelectorClass + " "
+		case style.Mode() == chroma.Light:
+			prefix = ".light "
+		case style.Mode() == chroma.Dark:
+			prefix = ".dark "
+		default:
+			return "", fmt.Errorf("style %q does not have a %q mode", style.Name, opts.Mode)
+		}
+		replacer := strings.NewReplacer(
+			".bg {", prefix+".bg {",
+			".chroma ", prefix+".chroma ",
+		)
+		css = replacer.Replace(css)
+	}
+
+	return css, nil
+}
+
+// isValidCSSClassName reports whether s is a simple CSS class name,
+// i.e. letters, digits, hyphens and underscores not starting with a digit.
+func isValidCSSClassName(s string) bool {
+	if s == "" {
+		return false
+	}
+	for i, r := range s {
+		switch {
+		case r >= 'a' && r <= 'z', r >= 'A' && r <= 'Z', r == '_', r == '-':
+		case r >= '0' && r <= '9' && i > 0:
+		default:
+			return false
+		}
+	}
+	return true
+}
+
+// chromaCSSOverrides re-emits leaf token colors that Chroma's minifier drops
+// because they equal the style's default foreground (the .chroma color). Without
+// modeSelector scoping, a paired light/dark stylesheet shares the same .chroma
+// scope, and the light sheet's explicit rule (e.g. .chroma .nx) would otherwise
+// leak into dark mode, since an explicit declaration beats inheritance.
+func chromaCSSOverrides(style *chroma.Style) map[chroma.TokenType]string {
+	bg := style.Get(chroma.Background)
+	m := make(map[chroma.TokenType]string)
+	for tt := range chroma.StandardTypes {
+		if tt == chroma.Background || !style.Has(tt) || !chromaLeafToken(tt) {
+			continue
+		}
+		entry := style.Get(tt)
+		if !entry.Sub(bg).IsZero() || !entry.Colour.IsSet() {
+			continue
+		}
+		if css := html.StyleEntryToCSS(chroma.StyleEntry{Colour: entry.Colour}); css != "" {
+			m[tt] = css
+		}
+	}
+	return m
+}
+
+func chromaLeafToken(tt chroma.TokenType) bool {
+	for other := range chroma.StandardTypes {
+		if other != tt && (other.Category() == tt || other.SubCategory() == tt) {
+			return false
+		}
+	}
+	return true
+}

+package highlight
+
+import (
+	"testing"
+
+	qt "github.com/frankban/quicktest"
+)
+
+func TestChromaStylesCSS(t *testing.T) {
+	c := qt.New(t)
+
+	css, err := ChromaStylesCSS(ChromaStylesOptions{Style: "Monokai"})
+	c.Assert(err, qt.IsNil)
+	c.Assert(css, qt.Contains, "/* GenericSubheading */")
+	c.Assert(css, qt.Not(qt.Contains), ".dark ")
+
+	css, err = ChromaStylesCSS(ChromaStylesOptions{Style: "monokai", OmitClassComments: true})
+	c.Assert(err, qt.IsNil)
+	c.Assert(css, qt.Not(qt.Contains), "GenericSubheading")
+
+	// Same-colour leaf tokens are kept without a mode selector.
+	css, err = ChromaStylesCSS(ChromaStylesOptions{Style: "github-dark"})
+	c.Assert(err, qt.IsNil)
+	c.Assert(css, qt.Contains, ".chroma .nx { color:#e6edf3 }")
+
+	css, err = ChromaStylesCSS(ChromaStylesOptions{Style: "github", Mode: "dark", ModeSelector: true})
+	c.Assert(err, qt.IsNil)
+	c.Assert(css, qt.Contains, ".dark .bg {")
+	c.Assert(css, qt.Contains, ".dark .chroma ")
+
+	css, err = ChromaStylesCSS(ChromaStylesOptions{Style: "github", ModeSelector: true})
+	c.Assert(err, qt.IsNil)
+	c.Assert(css, qt.Contains, ".light .chroma ")
+
+	css, err = ChromaStylesCSS(ChromaStylesOptions{Style: "github", Mode: "dark", ModeSelectorClass: "night"})
+	c.Assert(err, qt.IsNil)
+	c.Assert(css, qt.Contains, ".night .chroma ")
+	c.Assert(css, qt.Not(qt.Contains), ".dark ")
+
+	css, err = ChromaStylesCSS(ChromaStylesOptions{
+		Style:                  "monokai",
+		HighlightStyle:         "#fff000 bg:#000fff",
+		LineNumbersInlineStyle: "#111111",
+		LineNumbersTableStyle:  "#222222",
+	})
+	c.Assert(err, qt.IsNil)
+	c.Assert(css, qt.Contains, ".chroma .hl { color:#fff000;background-color:#000fff }")
+	c.Assert(css, qt.Contains, ".chroma .ln { white-space:pre;-webkit-user-select:none;user-select:none;margin-right:0.4em;padding:0 0.4em 0 0.4em;color:#111 }")
+	c.Assert(css, qt.Contains, ".chroma .lnt { white-space:pre;-webkit-user-select:none;user-select:none;margin-right:0.4em;padding:0 0.4em 0 0.4em;color:#222 }")
+
+	_, err = ChromaStylesCSS(ChromaStylesOptions{Style: "nope"})
+	c.Assert(err, qt.ErrorMatches, "invalid style: nope")
+	_, err = ChromaStylesCSS(ChromaStylesOptions{Style: "github", Mode: "dusk"})
+	c.Assert(err, qt.ErrorMatches, "invalid mode: dusk")
+	_, err = ChromaStylesCSS(ChromaStylesOptions{Style: "friendly", Mode: "dark"})
+	c.Assert(err, qt.ErrorMatches, `style "friendly" does not have a "dark" mode`)
+	_, err = ChromaStylesCSS(ChromaStylesOptions{Style: "github", ModeSelectorClass: "1a"})
+	c.Assert(err, qt.ErrorMatches, `invalid mode selector class name: "1a"`)
+}

+
+func TestChromaStyles(t *testing.T) {
+	t.Parallel()
+
+	files := `
+-- hugo.toml --
+disableKinds = ["page", "section", "taxonomy", "term", "sitemap", "rss"]
+[markup.highlight]
+style = "github"
+-- layouts/home.html --
+{{ $default := css.ChromaStyles (dict "targetPath" "css/chroma_default.css") }}
+Default: {{ $default.RelPermalink }}|{{ $default.MediaType }}|
+{{ $dark := css.ChromaStyles (dict "targetPath" "css/chroma_dark.css" "style" "github" "mode" "dark" "modeSelector" true) }}
+Dark: {{ $dark.RelPermalink }}|
+{{ $light := css.ChromaStyles (dict "targetPath" "/css/chroma_light.css" "style" "github" "mode" "light" "modeSelector" true "omitClassComments" true) }}
+Light: {{ $light.RelPermalink }}|
+{{ $custom := css.ChromaStyles (dict "targetPath" "css/chroma_custom.css" "style" "monokai" "modeSelector" "night" "highlightStyle" "#fff000 bg:#000fff") }}
+Custom: {{ $custom.RelPermalink }}|
+{{ $issue := css.ChromaStyles (dict "targetPath" "css/croma_dark.css" "style" "github" "mode" "dark" "modeSelector" "dark") }}
+Issue: {{ $issue.RelPermalink }}|
+`
+
+	b := hugolib.Test(t, files)
+
+	b.AssertFileContent("public/index.html",
+		"Default: /css/chroma_default.css|text/css|",
+		"Dark: /css/chroma_dark.css|",
+		"Light: /css/chroma_light.css|",
+		"Custom: /css/chroma_custom.css|",
+		"Issue: /css/croma_dark.css|",
+	)
+
+	// Style defaults to markup.highlight.style; no mode selector.
+	b.AssertFileContent("public/css/chroma_default.css", "/* Background */ .bg { background-color:#f7f7f7; }")
+	b.AssertFileContent("public/css/chroma_dark.css", "/* Background */ .dark .bg {", ".dark .chroma ")
+	b.AssertFileContent("public/css/chroma_light.css", ".light .bg {", ".light .chroma ", "! Background")
+	b.AssertFileContent("public/css/chroma_custom.css", ".night .chroma .hl { color:#fff000;background-color:#000fff }")
+	b.AssertFileContent("public/css/croma_dark.css", ".dark .chroma ")
+
+	dark := b.FileContent("public/css/chroma_dark.css")
+	light := b.FileContent("public/css/chroma_light.css")
+	b.Assert(dark, qt.Not(qt.Equals), light)
+	b.Assert(strings.Contains(b.FileContent("public/css/chroma_default.css"), ".light "), qt.IsFalse)
+}

+func TestChromaStylesErrors(t *testing.T) {

+	for _, test := range []struct {

+		{"missing mode", `(dict "targetPath" "a.css" "style" "friendly" "mode" "dark")`, `style "friendly" does not have a "dark" mode`},
+		{"unknown option", `(dict "targetPath" "a.css" "styel" "monokai")`, "styel"},
+		{"invalid class", `(dict "targetPath" "a.css" "modeSelector" ".foo bar")`, "invalid mode selector class name"},
+		{"slash only target path", `(dict "targetPath" "/" "style" "monokai")`, "must provide a targetPath"},
+		{"empty mode selector", `(dict "targetPath" "a.css" "modeSelector" "")`, "got an empty string"},
+		{"internal mode selector class option", `(dict "targetPath" "a.css" "modeSelectorClass" "x")`, "modeSelectorClass"},

+		t.Run(test.name, func(t *testing.T) {
+			t.Parallel()
+			files := `
+-- hugo.toml --
+disableKinds = ["page", "section", "taxonomy", "term", "sitemap", "rss"]
+-- layouts/home.html --

+`
+			files = strings.ReplaceAll(files, "OPTS", test.opts)
+			b, err := hugolib.TestE(t, files)
+			b.Assert(err, qt.IsNotNil)
+			b.Assert(err.Error(), qt.Contains, test.want)
+		})
+	}
+}

@@ -0,0 +1,161 @@
+// Copyright 2026 The Hugo Authors. All rights reserved.

+// limitations under the License.

+package highlight
+
+import (
+	"bytes"
+	"fmt"
+	"slices"
+	"strings"
+
+	"github.com/alecthomas/chroma/v2"
+	"github.com/alecthomas/chroma/v2/formatters/html"
+	"github.com/alecthomas/chroma/v2/styles"
+)
+
+// ChromaStylesOptions holds options for ChromaStylesCSS.
+type ChromaStylesOptions struct {
+	// Highlighter style, e.g. "monokai".
+	Style string
+
+	// Style mode, "light" or "dark".
+	Mode string
+
+	// Scope selectors under a top level mode class, e.g. ".dark .chroma".
+	ModeSelector bool
+
+	// Foreground and background colors for highlighted lines, e.g. "#fff000 bg:#000fff".
+	HighlightStyle string
+
+	// Foreground and background colors for inline line numbers.
+	LineNumbersInlineStyle string
+
+	// Foreground and background colors for table line numbers.
+	LineNumbersTableStyle string
+
+	// Omit CSS class comment prefixes in the generated CSS.
+	OmitClassComments bool
+}
+
+// ChromaStylesCSS generates a CSS stylesheet for the Chroma code highlighter.
+// This stylesheet is needed if markup.highlight.noClasses is disabled in config.
+func ChromaStylesCSS(opts ChromaStylesOptions) (string, error) {
+	name := strings.ToLower(opts.Style)
+	if !slices.Contains(styles.Names(), name) {
+		return "", fmt.Errorf("invalid style: %s", name)
+	}
+	var chromaStyle *chroma.Style
+	if opts.Mode != "" {
+		var mode chroma.Mode
+		switch opts.Mode {
+		case "light":
+			mode = chroma.Light
+		case "dark":
+			mode = chroma.Dark
+		default:
+			return "", fmt.Errorf("invalid mode: %s", opts.Mode)
+		}
+
+		chromaStyle = styles.GetForMode(name, mode)
+		if chromaStyle.Mode() != mode {
+			return "", fmt.Errorf("style %q does not have a %q mode", name, opts.Mode)
+		}
+	} else {
+		chromaStyle = styles.Get(name)
+	}
+	builder := chromaStyle.Builder()
+	if opts.HighlightStyle != "" {
+		builder.Add(chroma.LineHighlight, opts.HighlightStyle)
+	}
+	if opts.LineNumbersInlineStyle != "" {
+		builder.Add(chroma.LineNumbers, opts.LineNumbersInlineStyle)
+	}
+	if opts.LineNumbersTableStyle != "" {
+		builder.Add(chroma.LineNumbersTable, opts.LineNumbersTableStyle)
+	}
+	style, err := builder.Build()
+	if err != nil {
+		return "", err
+	}
+
+	options := []html.Option{
+		html.WithCSSComments(!opts.OmitClassComments),
+	}
+	if !opts.ModeSelector {
+		// Only needed for the shared-scope overlay; modeSelector
+		// gives each mode its own scope and makes this redundant.
+		options = append(options, html.WithCustomCSS(chromaCSSOverrides(style)))
+	}
+
+	var buf bytes.Buffer
+	if err := html.New(options...).WriteCSS(&buf, style); err != nil {
+		return "", err
+	}
+	css := buf.String()
+	if opts.ModeSelector {
+		// Scope every selector under a top level mode class, e.g. ".dark .chroma".
+		// This allows generating both light and dark stylesheets and toggling
+		// them with a parent class on the page.
+		// There's no upstream option for this (I think), so do string replacements for now.
+		// TODO(bep) upstream option for this.
+		var prefix string
+		switch style.Mode() {
+		case chroma.Light:
+			prefix = ".light "
+		case chroma.Dark:
+			prefix = ".dark "
+		default:
+			return "", fmt.Errorf("style %q does not have a light or dark mode", style.Name)
+		}
+		replacer := strings.NewReplacer(
+			".bg {", prefix+".bg {",
+			".chroma ", prefix+".chroma ",
+		)
+		css = replacer.Replace(css)
+	}
+
+	return css, nil
+}
+
+// chromaCSSOverrides re-emits leaf token colors that Chroma's minifier drops
+// because they equal the style's default foreground (the .chroma color). Without
+// modeSelector scoping, a paired light/dark stylesheet shares the same .chroma
+// scope, and the light sheet's explicit rule (e.g. .chroma .nx) would otherwise
+// leak into dark mode, since an explicit declaration beats inheritance.
+func chromaCSSOverrides(style *chroma.Style) map[chroma.TokenType]string {
+	bg := style.Get(chroma.Background)
+	m := make(map[chroma.TokenType]string)
+	for tt := range chroma.StandardTypes {
+		if tt == chroma.Background || !style.Has(tt) || !chromaLeafToken(tt) {
+			continue
+		}
+		entry := style.Get(tt)
+		if !entry.Sub(bg).IsZero() || !entry.Colour.IsSet() {
+			continue
+		}
+		if css := html.StyleEntryToCSS(chroma.StyleEntry{Colour: entry.Colour}); css != "" {
+			m[tt] = css
+		}
+	}
+	return m
+}
+
+func chromaLeafToken(tt chroma.TokenType) bool {
+	for other := range chroma.StandardTypes {
+		if other != tt && (other.Category() == tt || other.SubCategory() == tt) {
+			return false
+		}
+	}
+	return true
+}

+func TestChromaStyles(t *testing.T) {
+	t.Parallel()

+	files := `
+-- hugo.toml --
+disableKinds = ["taxonomy", "term", "rss", "sitemap", "section", "page"]
+[markup.highlight]
+style = "monokai"
+-- layouts/home.html --
+{{ $light := css.ChromaStyles (dict "targetPath" "css/chroma-light.css" "style" "github" "mode" "light" "modeSelector" true) }}
+{{ $dark := css.ChromaStyles (dict "targetPath" "css/chroma-dark.css" "style" "github" "mode" "dark" "modeSelector" true) }}
+{{ $default := css.ChromaStyles (dict "targetPath" "css/chroma.css") }}
+Light: {{ $light.RelPermalink }}|Dark: {{ $dark.RelPermalink }}|Default: {{ $default.RelPermalink }}|
+`
+
+	b := hugolib.Test(t, files)
+
+	b.AssertFileContent("public/index.html", "Light: /css/chroma-light.css|Dark: /css/chroma-dark.css|Default: /css/chroma.css|")

+	b.AssertFileContent("public/css/chroma.css", "/* Background */ .bg {", "background-color:#272822")

+disableKinds = ["taxonomy", "term", "rss", "sitemap", "section", "page"]
+-- layouts/home.html --

+`
+
+	for _, test := range []struct {
+		opts  string
+		match string
+	}{
+		{`(dict "style" "monokai")`, `.*targetPath cannot be empty.*`},
+		{`(dict "targetPath" "css/chroma.css" "style" "doesnotexist")`, `.*invalid style: doesnotexist.*`},
+		{`(dict "targetPath" "css/chroma.css" "mode" "blue")`, `.*invalid mode: blue.*`},
+		{`(dict "targetPath" "css/chroma.css" "style" "friendly" "mode" "dark")`, `.*style "friendly" does not have a "dark" mode.*`},
+	} {
+		files := strings.ReplaceAll(filesTemplate, "OPTS", test.opts)

title: common/hugo: Include aom, dav1d, and libavif in commands/env output

judge.reasoning: Both patches add the three requested libraries to GetDependencyListNonGo and both pass the independent tests, so correctness is equal. On tests, B is stronger: it adds a unit test in common/hugo/hugo_test.go and extends the env testscript to assert the exact name="version" strings for all four libraries, including under --logLevel info; A's testscript only checks that the module paths appear, not the versions, so a wrong or empty version would slip through. On scope, A goes beyond the ask by adding KaTeX (neutral) but also includes unrelated formatting churn in internal/warpc/warpc.go (re-wrapping closing parentheses of three unrelated calls), which is noise and counts against it; it also introduces a new cross-package dependency from common/hugo to internal/warpc. A's placement of version constants next to the code they describe with 'keep in sync' comments is a genuine craft advantage, but the values are still hand-maintained constants, so it is not a root-cause improvement over B's equivalent 'keep in sync with the Makefiles' comment. Weighing stronger, more precise tests and a tighter diff against A's nicer constant placement plus unrelated churn, B is the better fix.

title: resources/jsconfig: Address VS Code linting notice in jsconfig.json

judge.reasoning: Patch A fixes the root cause: every mapping emitted into compilerOptions.paths is made relative (prefixed with './' unless it already starts with '..'), which is exactly what the VS Code/TypeScript rule demands when baseUrl is unset. It covers the project's own assets ('./*'), themes/modules ('../...'), and nested mounts inside assets ('./sub/*'). Patch B instead sidesteps the symptom by dropping the mapping for the current directory, so in the single-root case no jsconfig.json is written at all. That avoids the lint notice for the simplest site but leaves any other root that resolves to a non-'..' relative path (e.g. a mount whose source lies inside assets, yielding 'sub/*') still non-relative and still flagged. The independent tests confirm this: both patches pass the project-only and theme scenarios, but only A passes the nested-mount scenario while B fails it. B also silently changes behaviour (no file emitted) rather than fixing the content. Tests: A adds a dedicated test asserting the relative forms for mixed roots plus the JSON shape, which would fail on base; B's added assertion only checks the nil case. Scope and craft: A's helper is small, documented, and uses filepath.Separator consistently with the existing filepath.Rel usage; the docs/assets/jsconfig.json tweak is a trivial, consistent companion change. A is clearly the better fix.

title: Panic when deleting a directory in static when server is running

judge.reasoning: Both patches address the same two-part root cause: (1) SourceFilesystem.Contains depended on the mount directory still existing on disk, so IsStatic returned false for a removed static directory and the event leaked into the dynamic rebuild path, and (2) processPartialFileEvents' component switch had no case for static. The independent tests confirm both patches fix every scenario (subdir, nested dir, root, mounted dir, rename, mixed batch). The difference is in how they get there. Patch B's Contains is a two-line reuse of the existing ReverseLookup(filename, false) machinery, which is already stat-free and already handles mounts, overlays and single-file mounts consistently with the rest of BaseFs; its switch change is the minimal, self-documenting 'handled by the static file syncer' case that keeps the rest of the loop (path parsing, cache-buster compilation) untouched. Patch A instead adds a new public RootMappingFs.MountDirs API, reimplements prefix matching by walking the filesystem stack and comparing r.To and r.Meta.Component, and restructures the pss loop to drop static paths entirely before cache-buster compilation. That is more surface area and more behavioural change than the issue asks for, and the early `continue` silently excludes static paths from cache busting rather than just from the component switch; it also leaves the original switch panic in place for any static path that might still arrive by another route. On tests, Patch A's Go rebuild tests (TestRunning + RemoveFiles for subdir and root deletion) are deterministic and directly mirror the issue, and its basefs unit test pins the Contains contract; these are stronger than Patch B's timing-based testscripts (`sleep 2`, `! stderr .`), which also only exercise module.mounts cases rather than a plain static/ subdirectory. That test advantage is real but does not outweigh B's cleaner, lower-risk fix: B resolves the root cause with less new code, better reuse of existing abstractions, and no change to the handling of non-static events, so B is the better patch.

title: related: Add option to tokenize headings

judge.reasoning: Patch A implements exactly what the issue specifies: `tokenize` only affects heading titles in `fragments` indices (the tokenizing helper is only invoked inside the `TypeFragments` branch), heading identifiers are still indexed as `FragmentKeyword` alongside new `FragmentTokenKeyword` tokens, so exact-identifier matching (e.g. `pagerefs: ['something-else']`) keeps working with tokenize on, and definition terms are untouched. It strips HTML tags and unescapes entities before splitting (heading titles like `Running hugo` tokenize correctly), respects `ToLower`, dedups tokens per document, and extends the `applyFilter` path with a distinct keyword type so filtered headings are computed by re-tokenizing titles. It adds docs, a config-decode assertion, a unit test for the tokenizer, and an integration test covering on/off, HTML in headings, definition terms, and exact-ID matching. Patch B diverges from the spec and has correctness bugs. It applies tokenization to basic indices via `ToKeywords` (string and []string), contradicting "Currently applies to heading titles in indices of type `fragments`"; the independent test TestBtJudgeTokenizeScopedToFragmentsIndices fails on B for exactly this reason. When tokenize is on it `continue`s past the heading identifier, so headings are no longer indexed by ID, breaking cross-page exact-identifier references on that index. Tokens are produced via `stringToKeyword` (a `StringKeyword`), yet the applyFilter branch only collects words from `kw.(FragmentKeyword)`, so `ff.words` is never populated and heading filtering silently stops working with tokenize enabled; B's own TestRelatedFragmentsTokenizeApplyFilter appears unable to pass as written. `splitWords` does not strip HTML tags, so a title containing `hugo` yields a garbage token like `em>hugo

issue_md:
See <https://discourse.gohugo.io/t/related-posts-based-on-heading/57467>.

I suggest using the name `tokenize`, documented as follows:

> (`bool`) Whether to split multi-word values into individual keywords for indexing and matching. Currently applies to heading titles in indices of type `fragments`; non-heading fragments such as definition terms continue to use exact-identifier matching regardless of this setting. This increases index size in proportion to the average number of words per heading; use `cardinalityThreshold` to prune common words and reduce build time. Default is `false`.

+// splitWords splits s into normalized words, stripping HTML entities and
+// leading/trailing punctuation from each word.
+func splitWords(title string) []string {
+	// Fast path: no whitespace or HTML entities means at most one token.
+	if strings.IndexFunc(title, unicode.IsSpace) == -1 && strings.IndexByte(title, '&') == -1 {
+		title = strings.TrimFunc(html.UnescapeString(title), func(r rune) bool { return !unicode.IsLetter(r) && !unicode.IsDigit(r) })
+		if title == "" {
+			return nil
+		}
+		return []string{title}
+	}
+	raw := strings.Fields(html.UnescapeString(title))
+	words := raw[:0]
+	for _, w := range raw {
+		w = strings.TrimFunc(w, func(r rune) bool { return !unicode.IsLetter(r) && !unicode.IsDigit(r) })
+		if w != "" {

title: panic: slice bounds out of range in contentNodeShifter.Delete when removing draft pages from a multilingual taxonomy

judge.reasoning: Both patches make the same core fix: the contentNodes branch of Delete/DeleteFunc previously mutated the slice in place while ranging over it (append(v[:i], v[i+1:]...)), so a second match at a stale index caused the out-of-bounds panic, and the shrunken slice header was never written back to the tree. Both rewrite this to build a fresh remaining slice, extend the Shifter interface to return the updated value, and have NodeShiftTree.delete/DeleteFuncRaw re-insert the updated node when something was deleted but the entry is not empty. The independent tests confirm both resolve the panic identically. The differences are in tests and craft. Patch A's test only exercises the shifter in isolation, so it would not catch a missing write-back in nodeshifttree.go, which is half of the fix. Patch B's tests drive the real NodeShiftTree via Shape(vec).Delete and DeleteFuncRaw, assert via GetRaw that the remaining nodes are actually persisted, that the key is removed once empty, and add a case for a contentNodesMap nested inside contentNodes losing only one dimension, plus an adjacent-match DeleteFunc case. Patch B also preallocates the remaining slice and documents why a new slice is required (shared backing array with the header stored in the tree), making the intent clearer to future readers. Patch A's nil-initialized remaining is functionally fine but offers no explanation. Scope is identical. B is the better patch on test strength and clarity.

issue_md:
### What version of Hugo are you using?

Reproduced on both:

```
hugo v0.159.1-86c7d3afacab79dc53325602d77ef884b7570268+extended darwin/arm64
hugo v0.164.0+extended+withdeploy darwin/arm64
```

### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release?

Yes (0.164.0).

### What did you expect to see?

A production build (no `-D`) of a multilingual site containing draft pages completes.

### What did you see instead?

```
panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [5:4]

goroutine 37 [running]:
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib.(*contentNodeShifter).Delete(0x..., {0x..., 0x...}, {0x2, 0x0, 0x0})
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/content_map_page_contentnodeshifter.go:48 +0x5f4
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/doctree.(*NodeShiftTree[...]).delete(0x..., {0x..., 0x35})
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/doctree/nodeshifttree.go:165 +0x84
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/doctree.(*NodeShiftTree[...]).Delete(...)
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/doctree/nodeshifttree.go:107
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib.(*allPagesAssembler).createAllPages.func1-range1(...)
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/content_map_page_assembler.go:106 +0xa4
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib.(*allPagesAssembler).createAllPages(...)
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/content_map_page_assembler.go:138 +0x168
github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib.(*HugoSites).assemble(...)
	github.com/gohugoio/hugo/hugolib/hugo_sites_build.go:345 +0x41c
```

The `0x35` in `delete(..., {…, 0x35})` is 53, exactly the byte length of the key being removed (`/blog/` plus a 47-character slug).

### Only on the page-removal path

`hugo -D` (drafts included) builds fine. The panic appears only when a page is *removed* from the tree, which makes it invisible in local preview and fatal only in production.

A **future `publishDate`** panics identically. Setting `[_build] render = "never"` / `list = "never"` on the same pages avoids it entirely — consistent with those pages never being added to the tree, so nothing is deleted.

### What I ruled out

Site: 8 languages, ~1,490 pages per language, ~11,455 content files, `categories` taxonomy.

- **Not a regression.** 0.159.1 and 0.164.0 behave identically.
- **Not the number of drafts.** 96 draft pages build fine; 16 panic.
- **Not slug length.** The panicking key was 47 chars, but renaming an unrelated post to exactly 47 chars builds fine.
- **Not the slug.** Renaming the offending page does not help.
- **Not byte layout.** Deleting a front-matter line, or adding a blank one, still panics.

Swapping page *content* at a fixed path isolates it to **front matter**. Changing `categories = ["Airport Operations"]` on the offending page to any other value clears the panic — and so does moving a *different* page out of that same category while leaving the offending one alone. So the trigger is combinatorial: some particular set of pages being deleted from one taxonomy term corrupts the shifter, rather than any single page being malformed.

### Reproducer

I have not managed to minimise it, and I want to be upfront about that. Synthetic multilingual sites (8 languages, 12 blog + 200 glossary pages sharing one taxonomy term, varying draft counts) do **not** reproduce, so something else in the real tree is required. The affected repository is private.

I am happy to run patches or instrumented builds against the real site and report back, which may be faster than guessing at a minimal case.

title: Add resources.Publish

judge.reasoning: The production code in the two patches is effectively identical: both register `Publish` on the resources namespace via AddMethodMapping and implement it by asserting the input to resource.Source, calling its Publish method, and returning the original resource (with a typed error for non-publishable inputs). Both satisfy the issue's ask, and all four independent tests pass on both. The differences are in tests, docs, and craft. Patch A's integration test covers more of the realistic surface: a plain asset, a minified (transformed) asset whose published name differs from its Name, a resources.Copy'd resource landing at the new target path, and a page resource in a bundle with publishResources disabled, plus a negative assertion that the untransformed copy source was not published. Patch B tests only the single minify pipeline case. Patch A also adds the user-facing docs page and the docs.yaml entry, which matches how the surrounding tpl functions are documented in this repository and is part of a complete feature addition; B adds none. A's doc comment is more descriptive and mirrors the issue's example. Neither patch adds risky scope. On tests and craft, A is the stronger patch.

title: Upgrade to Go 1.27

judge.reasoning: Both patches bump CI, go.mod, Dockerfile and run a sync of the forked text/html template packages. The decisive difference is the completeness of the html/template sync. Patch A brings in the full Go 1.27 JS-context changes: brace tracking resets jsCtx, `${` in a template literal resets jsCtx to regexp, `yield` is added to regexpPrecederKeywords with the property-access (`x.yield`, `x?.yield`, `x.in`) and private-identifier (`#yield`) exclusions in nextJSCtx and tJS, plus matching upstream tests (TestIssue81821, TestIssue81823, new TestEscapeText cases, TestNextJsCtx cases) and a Hugo-level integration test. Patch B only picks up the brace-depth part (CVE test) and omits the yield and `${` fixes, so its fork still diverges from Go 1.27 on security-relevant escaping. The independent tests confirm this: A passes all seven, B fails the yield, template-literal-substitution and site-level escaping tests while the others pass. On scope, B adds a lot of unrelated churn (herrors.Or replacing cmp.Or, a CopyDir behaviour change, a vectorstores refactor from errors to panics, warpc mutex and ErrShutdown handling, golden image updates, Alpine bump, removal of debug code, mass reformatting of test files). Some of these may be motivated by Go 1.27 toolchain changes, but they are not explained, cannot be verified here, and the vectorstores/warpc changes add behavioural risk beyond the issue's ask. B's fork-script improvements are nice housekeeping but do not offset an incomplete sync. A delivers the checklist's 'Synch template packages' item correctly with focused tests; B leaves it partially done.
