title: templates.Defer: identical block bodies in different output formats share one escaping mode, chosen non-deterministically per build

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the root cause the same way: they fold the owning template's IsPlainText into the deferred template ID so HTML and plain-text templates with identical bodies no longer collide, while same-format sharing (the documented key/hash cache behaviour the issue asks to preserve) is kept. All four independent tests derived from the issue's main reproduction and controls pass on both. The difference is where the escaping mode is read from. Patch A uses c.t.D.IsPlainText, but handleWithPartial creates a fresh transform context whose t is the partial template, so a deferred block nested inside a `with partial ... templates.Inner` decorator is keyed by the partial's (HTML) mode rather than the real owner's. That leaves exactly the issue's failure mode intact for that path, and the independent decorator test confirms it: FAIL-ASSERT on base and on A, PASS on B. Patch B tracks a deferOwner through the decorator sub-context and copies its deferNodes back to the owner, so the ID is always derived from the template whose escaping mode will actually be used in addDeferredTemplate. Tests: A adds one single-build test; B adds a 10-iteration test for the flip (appropriate since the bug was map-order dependent), a decorator test, and an explicit regression test that same-format identical blocks still share one execution, which directly guards the constraint the issue called out. B's extra plumbing is small, well-commented and scoped to the same mechanism, so it adds little risk. B is the more correct and better-tested fix.

issue_md:
### What version of Hugo are you using (`hugo version`)? 
$ hugo version
hugo v0.164.0-ce2470e7012b5ab5fc4e10ebe4027e9f8d9e00dc+extended windows/amd64 BuildDate=2026-07-06T16:39:30Z VendorInfo=gohugoio
### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release? Yes. ```text hugo v0.165.0-76a5e1880ab46688155b02e99bab9be2a6134492+extended windows/amd64 BuildDate=2026-08-12T14:26:28Z VendorInfo=gohugoio ``` Over one run of 40 consecutive builds of the unchanged reproduction site below with that binary, 28 builds published the wrong value in `public/index.html` and 12 published the wrong value in `public/index.txt`. All 40 exited 0, and none printed a warning or an error. ### Summary When two templates belonging to different output formats contain byte-identical `templates.Defer` block bodies, both blocks do execute, each with its own correct output-format context. What they share is the escaping applied inside the block, and which of the two escaping modes survives changes from build to build of an unchanged site. On every build exactly one of the two outputs is therefore wrong: either an HTML page publishes a value raw that it escapes correctly a few characters earlier outside the block, or a plain-text page receives HTML entities. ### Reproduction Three files in an empty directory. No content, no modules, no external tooling. `hugo.toml`: ```toml baseURL = 'https://example.org/' title = 'defer probe' disableKinds = ['page', 'section', 'taxonomy', 'term', 'RSS', 'sitemap', 'robotsTXT'] [outputFormats.probe] mediaType = 'text/plain' baseName = 'index' isPlainText = true [outputs] home = ['html', 'probe'] ``` `layouts/home.html`: ```go-html-template {{ $v := "&" }}OUT[{{ $v }}]{{ with (templates.Defer (dict "key" "K" "data" (dict "v" $v))) }}IN[{{ .v }}]{{ end }} ``` `layouts/home.probe.txt`, byte-identical to `layouts/home.html` (both md5 `c921197a9c8637852e38d94a0352359d`): ```go-html-template {{ $v := "&" }}OUT[{{ $v }}]{{ with (templates.Defer (dict "key" "K" "data" (dict "v" $v))) }}IN[{{ .v }}]{{ end }} ``` `OUT[...]` interpolates the value outside the deferred block, `IN[...]` interpolates the same value inside it. Then run `hugo` several times without changing anything, and look at `public/index.html` and `public/index.txt` after each run. ### What happens Two consecutive runs of the same command on the unchanged site, pasted verbatim: ```text $ hugo --logLevel info Start building sites … hugo v0.164.0-ce2470e7012b5ab5fc4e10ebe4027e9f8d9e00dc+extended windows/amd64 BuildDate=2026-07-06T16:39:30Z VendorInfo=gohugoio INFO build: step process substep collect files 0 files_total 0 pagesources_total 0 resourcesources_total 0 duration 0s INFO build: step process duration 0s INFO build: step assemble duration 0s INFO build: step render substep pages site en outputFormat html duration 1.3703ms INFO build: step render substep pages site en outputFormat probe duration 509.5µs INFO build: step render pages 2 content 0 duration 1.8798ms INFO build: step render deferred count 2 duration 1.7766ms INFO build: step postProcess duration 0s INFO build: duration 4.171ms │ EN ──────────────────┼──── Pages │ 2 Paginator pages │ 0 Non-page files │ 0 Static files │ 0 Processed images │ 0 Aliases │ 0 Cleaned │ 0 Total in 12 ms --- public/index.html --- OUT[<b>&]IN[&] --- public/index.txt --- OUT[&]IN[&] ``` ```text $ hugo --logLevel info Start building sites … hugo v0.164.0-ce2470e7012b5ab5fc4e10ebe4027e9f8d9e00dc+extended windows/amd64 BuildDate=2026-07-06T16:39:30Z VendorInfo=gohugoio INFO build: step process substep collect files 0 files_total 0 pagesources_total 0 resourcesources_total 0 duration 513.8µs INFO build: step process duration 513.8µs INFO build: step assemble duration 0s INFO build: step render substep pages site en outputFormat html duration 517.9µs INFO build: step render substep pages site en outputFormat probe duration 517.2µs INFO build: step render pages 2 content 0 duration 1.0351ms INFO build: step render deferred count 2 duration 2.0736ms INFO build: step postProcess duration 0s INFO build: duration 3.6225ms │ EN ──────────────────┼──── Pages │ 2 Paginator pages │ 0 Non-page files │ 0 Static files │ 0 Processed images │ 0 Aliases │ 0 Cleaned │ 0 Total in 12 ms --- public/index.html --- OUT[<b>&]IN[<b>&] --- public/index.txt --- OUT[&]IN[<b>&] ``` In the first run the HTML page publishes `&` raw inside the block, a few characters after escaping the same value correctly outside it. In the second run the plain-text page receives `<b>&`. Nothing changed between the two runs. Quantified over builds of the unchanged site, each build a separate one-shot `hugo` invocation: | Hugo version | builds | `index.html` published raw `&` inside the block | `index.txt` published `<b>&` inside the block | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | v0.164.0, fresh copy of the site per build | 40 | 25 | 15 | | v0.164.0, fresh copy of the site per build, second run | 40 | 23 | 17 | | v0.165.0, fresh copy of the site per build | 40 | 26 | 14 | | v0.165.0, fresh copy of the site per build, second run | 40 | 28 | 12 | | v0.164.0, repeated builds in one directory | 12 | 8 | 4 | | v0.165.0, repeated builds in one directory | 8 | 5 | 3 | In all 180 of those builds the two output formats carried the *same* string inside the block, so exactly one of the two published files was wrong every time; outside the block the value was escaped correctly for its format in every build. ### What I expected Each format's deferred block rendered under that format's own escaping — `IN[<b>&]` in `public/index.html` and `IN[&]` in `public/index.txt` — and the same result on every build of an unchanged site. The documentation says "The output format, site, and language will be the same, even if the execution is deferred." The output-format *context* does hold up, as the identity-token control below shows; it is the escaping regime that does not follow the output format. ### Controls All of these were run at both v0.164.0 and v0.165.0. **The block really does execute once per output format.** Adding `{{ warnf "DEFER-EXEC-%d" math.Counter }}` to the start of the still byte-identical block body logs two executions in every build: ```text WARN DEFER-EXEC-1 WARN DEFER-EXEC-2 INFO build: step render deferred count 2 duration 1.7497ms --- public/index.html --- OUT[<b>&]IN[&] --- public/index.txt --- OUT[&]IN[&] ``` So this is not one rendering substituted into two files; it is two renderings sharing one escaping mode. **Different `key` values do not separate them.** With `"KH"` in `layouts/home.html` and `"KT"` in `layouts/home.probe.txt`, the block bodies still byte-identical, the escaping stayed shared and kept flipping: 36 builds, 22 with the HTML page wrong and 14 with the plain-text page wrong. **Different block body text does separate them, stably.** Changing the body to `INH[{{ .v }}]` in the HTML template and `INT[{{ .v }}]` in the plain-text template gives the correct per-format result in 36 of 36 builds, with no flip: `INH[<b>&]` in `public/index.html` and `INT[&]` in `public/index.txt`. **The per-format context inside the block is correct.** With the body still byte-identical in both templates, but carrying an output-format identity token next to the value: ```go-html-template {{ $v := "&" }}OUT[{{ $v }}]{{ with (templates.Defer (dict "key" "K" "data" (dict "v" $v))) }}IN[{{ (index page.AlternativeOutputFormats 0).Name }}|{{ .v }}]{{ end }} ``` With exactly two formats configured the single alternative names the *other* one, so `IN[probe|...]` marks the execution that produced the HTML page and `IN[html|...]` the one that produced the plain-text page. That token was correct in 36 of 36 builds, while the escaping of the value beside it in the very same body was shared and flipped across those builds: ```text public/index.html OUT[<b>&]IN[probe|&] public/index.txt OUT[&]IN[html|&] public/index.html OUT[<b>&]IN[probe|<b>&] public/index.txt OUT[&]IN[html|<b>&] ``` ### Where this appears to come from Offered as a lead from reading the source, not as an instrumented finding. `tpl/tplimpl/templatetransform.go`, `handleWith` (v0.164.0, function at line 409) registers the extracted block under a hash of the block body alone, at lines 450-459: ```go inner := withNode.List.CopyList() s := inner.String() ... innerHash := hashing.XxHashFromStringHexEncoded(s) deferredID := tpl.HugoDeferredTemplatePrefix + innerHash ... c.deferNodes[deferredID] = inner ``` Nothing about the owning template, its output format or its media type enters that identifier, so two templates in different output formats with the same body produce the same `deferredID`. `tpl/tplimpl/templatestore.go`, `addDeferredTemplate` (v0.164.0, function at line 916) then keeps only the first registration under that name, and the first owner fixes the parse namespace for whoever comes later: ```go if _, found := t.templatesByPath.Get(name); found { return nil } ... if owner.D.IsPlainText { prototype := t.tns.parseText ... } else { prototype := t.tns.parseHTML ... } ``` That is exactly the escaping regime the two output formats disagree about, and the loser silently inherits the winner's. Which owner gets there first looks order-dependent. `transformTemplates` (function at line 1916) reaches the registrations by ranging `s.templates()` at line 1937, and that iterator's inner loop at line 1784 ranges a `map[nodeKey]*TemplInfo` — the value type of `treeMain`, declared at line 447 — whose iteration order Go randomizes per run. I found no sort on that path. One contrast worth noting: the sibling transform in the same file, `handleWithPartial` (function at line 324), hashes the owning template's name into its identifier at line 335 — `hashing.XxHashFromStringHexEncoded(c.t.Name() + withNodeInnerString)` — while the older defer path does not. I checked the implicated files at v0.164.0, v0.165.0 and master `7b5199fdeff7d7682e9f979f468d55bc7b67b934`: `tpl/tplimpl/templatestore.go`, `tpl/templates/templates.go` and `tpl/template.go` are byte-identical at all three, and `tpl/tplimpl/templatetransform.go` differs at master only outside this path — the `handleWith` lines quoted above are unchanged there, at 405-414. ### A constraint on any fix Hashing the owning template's name into the deferred identifier, the way `handleWithPartial` does, would break something the documentation promises for `key`: "This will, combined with a hash of the template content, be used as a cache key." Two *different layouts of the same output format* with identical bodies and one shared key share a single execution today, and that is worth keeping — at both versions, on a variant of the site above reduced to one output format and with the `page` kind enabled plus one content file, so that `single.html` renders at all, I measured a single `DEFER-EXEC-1` for a `home.html` and a `single.html` written that way, with both pages publishing the shared result. Separating registrations by the property that actually differs here — the owner's `IsPlainText`, or its output format — would fix the escaping while leaving that documented same-format sharing untouched. ### Related, not duplicates - #7774, fixed by #8462 ("Fixes #7774", merged 2021-04-23): per-build nondeterminism in output-format template lookup for shortcodes. Same failure shape, different subsystem, and it predates `templates.Defer`. - #13236: two empty deferred blocks *in the same template* collided on the identifier `__hdeferred/cafc7706cee4572b` and panicked; closed as completed. That is the same body-only identifier, in a different situation — the collision there is inside one template, and the cross-output-format escaping consequence does not come up. I did not find an existing report covering byte-identical `templates.Defer` bodies across output formats. ### What I did not establish - **Which registration wins in any individual build.** I inferred the winner from the escaping in the published output; I did not instrument the running binary to observe the registration. - **Platform generality.** Everything above was measured on one machine, Windows 11, amd64 extended builds. Whether the split differs on another platform or core count is unmeasured. - **Two non-plain-text formats sharing a body.** The escaping observable needs an `isPlainText` format paired with an HTML one, so two HTML-ish formats sharing a body were not tested and the reach across format combinations is unknown.

title: hugo mod npm pack emits a publishable, checkout-named package.json

judge.reasoning: Both patches add "private": true and drop the checkout-basename name, so both fix the core publishability problem. B uses a fixed scoped name (@gohugoio/hugoautogen), which is exactly what the issue asks for ("Ideally the default is scoped"), is fully deterministic across checkouts, and also updates the docs. A chooses a bare default ("hugoautogen"), which the issue explicitly calls out as claimable by anyone on the registry, and layers on a preserve-existing-fields mechanism. That mechanism has a real downside for the issue's own scenario: a repo whose committed manifest was generated by an older Hugo (name "site-a", no private) will keep the checkout-derived name forever after upgrade, because A copies any non-empty existing name. The independent TestBtJudgePackFreshCloneOfPreviouslyPackedSite and TestBtJudgePackDefaultNameIsScoped fail on A and pass on B for precisely these reasons, and I confirmed from the diff that this is genuine behaviour, not a test artifact. A's preserve-fields behaviour is also beyond the issue's ask and adds risk (e.g. honoring private=false, silently carrying stale names). On tests, both add meaningful integration tests and update goldens; B's test additionally exercises two differently named checkouts and asserts byte-identical output, which directly matches the reported symptom. B is simpler, more correct against the issue text, and better tested.

issue_md:
**TL;DR**: the generated `package.json` has no `"private": true` and a checkout-derived `name`, so committed copies are publishable under names sites don't control. Suggested fix: emit `"private": true` and a stable (ideally scoped) default name.

### What version of Hugo are you using (`hugo version`)?

```
hugo v0.165.0-76a5e1880ab46688155b02e99bab9be2a6134492+extended darwin/arm64 BuildDate=2026-08-12T14:26:28Z VendorInfo=gohugoio
```

### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release?

Yes (transcript below is v0.165.0). The behavior is in master's [package_builder.go](https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/master/modules/npm/package_builder.go).

### What happened

`hugo mod npm pack` writes `packages/hugoautogen/package.json` with:

- a **name derived from the checkout directory**, so it varies per clone and can be a registry name the site doesn't control, and
- **no `"private": true`**, npm's do-not-publish guard for internal packages.

The file is regenerated wholesale on each run, so hand-set fields don't survive. From a fresh clone of a repo whose committed copy was hand-normalized:

```console
$ git clone https://github.com/google/docsy-example.git site-a && cd site-a
$ grep -E '"(name|version|private)"' packages/hugoautogen/package.json
  "name": "@docsy/hugoautogen",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "private": true
$ hugo mod npm pack
$ grep -E '"(name|version|private)"' packages/hugoautogen/package.json
  "name": "site-a",
  "version": "0.1.0"
```

A sibling clone of the same repo into `site-b` yields `"name": "site-b"`.

### Why it matters

Sites that commit the generated workspace (e.g. so `npm ci` works without running Hugo first) end up carrying a manifest that npm workspace publishing and common release tools treat as publishable by default: `npm publish --dry-run --workspaces` packs it as `site-a@0.1.0`, while with `"private": true` npm skips the workspace. The name variance also churns the committed manifest, and the lockfile's workspace entry, across differently named checkouts.

### What did you expect

The generated internal workspace is non-publishable (`"private": true`) and has a stable, project-controlled default name rather than the checkout directory's basename. Ideally the default is scoped: a bare name can be claimed on the registry by anyone, a scoped one only by the scope owner.

### Workaround

[docsy-example#487](https://github.com/google/docsy-example/pull/487) follows each pack invocation with a single `npm pkg set` line restoring a scoped name and `private`.

Happy to send a PR for the `private` field (and for the name default, if you have a preference for what it should be).

title: github: Fix workflow for stale issues

judge.reasoning: The failure is an input-validation bug in the pinned dessant/lock-threads action (it rejects tokens over 100 chars). Patch B addresses the root cause by bumping the pinned action to a newer release (v6.0.2) that lifts that limit, keeping all existing inputs, behavior, and the SHA-pinning convention intact. It is a one-line, low-risk change that matches the issue's ask exactly. Patch A instead rips out the action and reimplements its logic as an ad hoc bash script against the REST API. That is a far broader redesign than the issue calls for and introduces real behavioral and reliability risk: it caps each run at 50 items per type via per_page=50 with no pagination, so a backlog would never be cleared; the search query semantics (updated:<, is:unlocked, archived:false) only approximate the action's inactivity logic; it hardcodes lock_reason=resolved, which the original did not specify; and it changes the stale step to run with !cancelled(), masking failures in the new script. It also loses the maintained, pinned third-party behavior in favor of untested shell. Neither patch includes tests, which is expected for a workflow-only change. On correctness, scope, and craft, B is the better fix.

title: Consider bumping mainImageVersionNumber

judge.reasoning: The issue asks to bump mainImageVersionNumber so that cached results affected by the two filter/palette fixes are regenerated. Patch A does exactly that (1 -> 2) and also fixes a real gap: Filter() previously keyed only on the filter list, so no version bump could ever invalidate images.Filter results. A's ForFilters derives the filter key from the existing config key, which already carries both the main and per-format version numbers, so filtered images are now invalidated by any future bump as well. It adds a focused unit test that proves a bump changes both process and filter keys, and updates the dependent hash expectations and golden files consistently. Patch B does not bump the main version at all; it instead adds a PNG-only format version. That misses paletted GIF targets, which are squarely within the scope of the 'paletted images' and 'preserve the source palette for geometric filter chains' fixes, so a site with resized GIFs would still serve stale output. B also exports two previously internal variables just so image.go can rebuild the key by hand (duplicating the logic DecodeImageConfig already has, and inconsistently: no 'tfv' prefix), and it carries a large amount of unrelated reformatting churn of AssertFileContent calls across several test files, which obscures the actual change. The independent tests pass on both because they only exercise PNG, so they do not separate the patches, but on correctness against the issue's ask, scope, and craft, A is clearly the better fix. One caveat for A: the diff shows new golden webp/gif files but no deletions of the old ones; this may be an artifact of binary stripping, and I cannot confirm from the diff alone.

title: Improve/document security.http.urls override behavior

judge.reasoning: The issue asks to improve or better document the behavior where the dial-time private-address check is skipped when security.http.urls is customized. Patch A addresses exactly that: it factors the decision into HTTP.IsPrivateAddressAllowed, adds an explicit tri-state security.http.allowPrivateAddresses so users with a broad custom allowlist can keep the check (the reported security concern) and users with the default allowlist can opt out, and documents the whole mechanism in a dedicated 'Resolved address check' section with a warning and concrete examples. Its tests cover all four combinations at both the config level and the real transport, and would fail before the change. Patch B documents the existing behavior adequately (the independent docs test passes for both), but its code change is a different feature: it disables HTTP(S)_PROXY support by default and adds a proxyFromEnvironment knob. That is a breaking default-behavior change for users behind corporate proxies, is not what the issue asked for, and does nothing to let a user with a custom urls allowlist keep the private-address check. The proxy plumbing (context-carried proxy URL, canonicalAddr mirror, custom RoundTripper) adds nontrivial risk and surface area that obscures rather than improves the override behavior in question. Patch A is more correct for the stated issue, better tested for it, and tightly scoped.

issue_md:
In d6e6f9e500eebdeae8e28de830fff2e3bfc7d534 (unreleased) we added a dial-time URL validation to catch URLs that's valid according to the whitelist but that resolves to a loopback, private or link-local IP addresses. That check is skipped it if the user has a custom `security.http.urls` setup, as it would not make sense to block local development servers.

See `CheckAllowedHTTPAddress`.

This has been reported by @Reload3d  as a potential security issue, and while I think the current behaviour is the pragmatic correct approach, I'm creating this issue for visibility and to see if this can be improved further (e.g. better documentation).

+## Resolved address check
+
+{{< new-in 0.166.0 />}}
+
+The `http.urls` allowlist only inspects the URL text. A host name that passes the allowlist can still resolve to an internal address, such as `127.0.0.1`, `10.0.0.1`, or the cloud metadata endpoint `169.254.169.254`. To guard against this, Hugo checks the resolved IP address when `resources.GetRemote` opens a connection, and it refuses to connect to a loopback, private, link-local, or other non-public address.
+
+By default, Hugo applies this check only when `http.urls` has its default value. If you customize `http.urls`, Hugo assumes that you have chosen which hosts to allow, which may include a local development server or a host on your private network, and it skips the check.
+
+> [!WARNING]
+> If you customize `http.urls` with a broad pattern such as `.*`, and your templates fetch URLs that come from untrusted sources, such as front matter or data files, a host name that resolves to an internal address can make Hugo read from your private network. In that case, set `http.allowPrivateAddresses` to `false` to keep the check.
+
+> [!NOTE]
+> If you route requests through a proxy with the `HTTP_PROXY` or `HTTPS_PROXY` environment variables, Hugo checks the address of the proxy, not the address of the target host.
+

+
+```toml
+[security.http]
+urls = ['.*', '! ^https?://evil\.example\.com']
+allowPrivateAddresses = false
+```
+
+To keep the default `http.urls` allowlist and allow host names that resolve to internal addresses:
+
+```toml
+[security.http]
+allowPrivateAddresses = true
+```
+

title: js.Build should support es2025 as target

judge.reasoning: Both patches make the identical one-line root-cause fix: adding the "es2025" key mapping to api.ES2025 in the target lookup map in internal/js/esbuild/options.go. Both pass the independent tests equally. Both add the same unit-table entries in options_test.go (es2024 and es2025 cases), which would fail before and pass after. Patch B additionally adds an integration test (TestBuildTargetES2025) reproducing the issue's exact scenario (TypeScript asset, minify, sourceMap none, target es2025) and asserting the built output, which exercises the real js.Build template path rather than only the option-conversion function. Patch B also updates the user-facing docs list of valid targets, which was stale and is directly relevant since the issue complains the target is neither supported nor listed, and refreshes a stale code comment that still said es2015-es2020. None of B's extra changes add risk or obscure the fix. The integration test's exact-output assertion is somewhat brittle against future esbuild minifier changes, but that is a minor concern. B is the better patch on tests and scope completeness.

title: tpl/compare: eq, le and ge disagree when comparing an int with an equal float

judge.reasoning: Both patches make eq agree with lt/le/gt/ge for numerically equal int/float pairs; all four independent tests pass on both, so the issue itself is resolved either way. Patch A fixes the root inconsistency directly: Eq now applies the same int-to-float numeric rule that compareGet already uses, and it also closes a latent hole in compareGetWithCollator where a uint64 compared against a non-uint left `left`/`right` at zero. Its tests target the exact scenarios in the issue (1/1.0, 0/0.0, -1/-1.0, int64/float64, uint/float, both orders, multi-arg eq) and would fail on base. The remaining imprecision (int64 above 2^53 compared via float64) is shared with the pre-existing lt/gt path, so the API stays self-consistent, which is what the issue asks for. Patch B is a correct and more exact design (an integer-exact CompareNumbers used by Eq, compareGet and where), but it goes well beyond the ask in ways that add risk: it changes the documented semantics of hreflect.ConvertIfPossible (now rejects int64(MaxInt64)->float64, 1<<53+1->float64, float64(3.14)->float32, and no longer dereferences pointers), rewriting existing test expectations to match; this helper was added for YAML uint64 handling and is used by collections' convertNumber, so large-int-to-float conversions in collection functions can now start erroring. It also rewrites Eq's normalize, checkCondition in where.go, and the Comparer branches, and adds a ~100-line benchmark unrelated to the fix. None of that is needed to resolve the reported inconsistency, and it obscures the fix while introducing behaviour changes outside the issue. On correctness both resolve the issue; on tests both add meaningful failing-before tests (B's are broader); on scope A is tight while B's redesign carries real regression risk. A wins on balance.

issue_md:
### What version of Hugo are you using (`hugo version`)? 
$ hugo version
hugo v0.166.0-DEV-ae07063fcc9a59c95838e83e7fdf12e326ebee7d darwin/arm64
### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release? I built `master` at `ae07063` and reproduced it there. I did not run a tagged release binary, so I have not confirmed it against one directly, though the code path is unchanged in `tpl/compare/compare.go`. ### What did you expect to see? `eq`, `ne`, `lt`, `le`, `gt` and `ge` agreeing with each other. Whatever the rule for comparing an `int` against a `float`, exactly one of `lt`/`eq`/`gt` should hold for a given pair, `le` should mean `lt or eq`, and `ge` should mean `gt or eq`. ### What did you see instead? For `1` against `1.0`, the six functions contradict each other. `le` and `ge` are both true while `lt`, `gt` and `eq` are all false, so the value is reported as neither less than, nor greater than, nor equal to itself. `layouts/index.html`: ```go-html-template eq 1 1.0 = {{ eq 1 1.0 }} ne 1 1.0 = {{ ne 1 1.0 }} lt 1 1.0 = {{ lt 1 1.0 }} le 1 1.0 = {{ le 1 1.0 }} gt 1 1.0 = {{ gt 1 1.0 }} ge 1 1.0 = {{ ge 1 1.0 }} ``` Rendered output: ``` eq 1 1.0 = false ne 1 1.0 = true lt 1 1.0 = false le 1 1.0 = true gt 1 1.0 = false ge 1 1.0 = true ``` `eq` normalises an `int` to `int64` and a `float` to `float64` and then compares them as `any`, so they are never equal. `lt`/`le`/`gt`/`ge` go through `compareGet`, which converts both to `float64`, so they compare numerically. The two halves of the API use different rules. Same result for `0` vs `0.0`, `-1` vs `-1.0`, `int64(3)` vs `float64(3)` and `uint(4)` vs `4.0`. Mixed values where the numbers genuinely differ (`1` vs `2.0`) are consistent, so this only shows up when the two are numerically equal. This is adjacent to #3721, which asked for `eq` to be more lenient and was closed by the stale bot in 2018 without a decision. This report is narrower: whichever convention you prefer, the current combination is not self-consistent. I have not sent a patch because the fix is a semantics choice, either making `eq` compare numerically or making `le`/`ge` strict about mixed types, and that is your call. Happy to send a PR once you say which. This issue was written primarily by Claude Code, including the reproduction above.

title: tpl/collections: union silently returns an empty list when the two slice types differ

judge.reasoning: The issue asks that `union` return either the union or an error whenever the slice types differ, and it calls out three concrete cases: int/float, int/string, and the uncomparable `(slice (slice 1)) (slice 2)` case that the early return currently shadows. Patch A removes the early return at its root, converts l2 elements to l1's element type (numbers via convertNumber, strings via ToStringE, otherwise ConvertIfPossible), returns an explicit `union: unable to convert value of type X to Y` error when conversion is impossible, and moves the uncomparable-types check so it runs per element before any silent return. It also handles interface element types and nil values carefully. The independent tests confirm all four issue scenarios pass on A. Patch B only special-cases the numeric/numeric pair inside the existing early return; `union (slice 1) (slice "a")` still silently returns `[]`, and `union (slice (slice 1)) (slice 2)` still returns `[]` instead of the uncomparable error, both of which the independent tests show failing on B exactly as on base. B's own tests even enshrine the silent-empty behaviour (`[]string{"1","2"} ∪ []int{3} -> []string{}` and `[]int{} ∪ []float64{1.0} -> []int{}`), which is the behaviour the issue reports as the bug. On tests, A adds unit cases that flip the old silent-empty expectations to errors plus a template-level integration test covering the exact snippets from the issue, including error-message matches; B's tests only cover the numeric subset. A's scope is larger than a minimal error-return, but the issue explicitly offered the 'accept mixed types like intersect' direction, and the extra code is coherent and tested rather than risky churn. A also updates the doc comment, which previously stated an incorrect contract. A is clearly the better fix.

issue_md:
### What version of Hugo are you using (`hugo version`)? 
$ hugo version
hugo v0.166.0-DEV-ae07063fcc9a59c95838e83e7fdf12e326ebee7d darwin/arm64
### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release? I built `master` at `ae07063` and reproduced it there. I did not run a tagged release binary, so I have not confirmed it against one directly, though `Union` is unchanged in `tpl/collections/collections.go`. ### What did you expect to see? `union` either returning the union of its two arguments, or returning an error. It already errors for the other argument shapes it cannot handle, for example `union does not support slices or arrays of uncomparable types` and `can't iterate over ...`. ### What did you see instead? `union` returns an empty slice, with no error, whenever the two arguments have different slice types and neither has an interface element type. `layouts/index.html`: ```go-html-template {{ printf "%T" (slice 1) }} {{ printf "%T" (slice 1.0) }} union int,int -> {{ union (slice 1) (slice 2) }} union int,float -> {{ union (slice 1) (slice 1.0) }} union int,string -> {{ union (slice 1) (slice "a") }} union lists -> {{ union (slice 1 2) (slice 2.0 3.0) }} intersect lists -> {{ intersect (slice 1 2) (slice 2.0 3.0) }} ``` Output: ``` []int []float64 union int,int -> [1 2] union int,float -> [] union int,string -> [] union lists -> [] intersect lists -> [2] ``` `intersect` handles the same two mixed-type lists and returns `[2]`, so the sibling functions disagree about whether these arguments are usable at all. The cause is this early return in `Union`: ```go if l1v.Type() != l2v.Type() && l1v.Type().Elem().Kind() != reflect.Interface && l2v.Type().Elem().Kind() != reflect.Interface { return ins.r.Interface(), nil } ``` `ins.r` is the empty slice made just above, so a caller gets an empty list rather than an error. It is reachable from ordinary templates because `slice 1` is `[]int` and `slice 1.0` is `[]float64`, and it also runs before the uncomparable-types check, so `union (slice (slice 1)) (slice 2)` returns `[]` instead of the error that check would raise. Adding one element of another type to the first argument avoids it, since the slice then becomes `[]interface {}`: `union (slice 1 "x") (slice 1.0)` returns `[1 x]`. ### Stack traceback or browser console output None, no error is raised. That is the problem. --- This is a different mechanism from #3411, which was closed in 2017 and is now locked with a note asking that related bugs be opened as new issues. Happy to send a PR. Returning an error here would be a small change; making `union` accept mixed types the way `intersect` does is bigger, so I would rather you pick the direction first. title: tpl/transform: Strip BOM prior to unmarshaling a resource or string

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the issue at the same root: trimming the UTF-8 BOM at the top of metadecoders Decoder.Unmarshal, which is the path transform.Unmarshal uses for both resources and strings. The independent tests confirm both go from FAIL-ASSERT on base to PASS for CSV, JSON, TOML, YAML and XML, as resources and as strings, so correctness on the issue's scenarios is equal. The differences are in scope hygiene, tests, and craft. Patch A mixes in unrelated reformatting of existing test calls (splitting AssertFileContent and ReplaceAll argument lists across lines), which removes eight lines and adds noise that obscures the actual fix. Patch B keeps the existing tests untouched. Patch B also factors the BOM into a named constant and a small stripBOM helper instead of an inline byte literal with a trailing comment, and applies it consistently to UnmarshalTo and UnmarshalYaml and the i18n bundle; that extra coverage is beyond the ask and earns no credit on its own, but it is low risk (a trailing-whitespace-style prefix trim) and does not complicate the core change. On tests, both add a multi-format integration test that would fail before and pass after. B additionally includes the issue's own reproduction verbatim and exercises the site.Data path and i18n files, so its tests are broader without being tautological. A's test is adequate but narrower and ships alongside churn. Weighing scope (A's unrelated churn counts against it) and craft (B's named helper and constant), B is the better patch by a modest margin.

Reference: <https://discourse.gohugo.io/t/57561>

Although the forum topic above is about CSV data, I think we'd have the same/similar problem with JSON, XML, and TOML data.

Failing example:

```text
git clone --single-branch -b hugo-github-issue-15335 https://github.com/jmooring/hugo-testing hugo-github-issue-15335
cd hugo-github-issue-15335
hugo --ignoreCache && cat public/index.html
```

Expected:

```text
city: tokyo|country: japan|
fruit: apple|color: red|
id: 1234|role: developer|
vehicle: car|type: sedan|
name: laptop|price: 999.99|
```

Actual:

```text
city: |country: japan|
fruit: |color: red|
id: |role: developer|
vehicle: |type: sedan|
name: |price: 999.99|
```

func TestUnmarshalCSVWithBOM(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	bom := "\xef\xbb\xbf"

	files := `
-- hugo.toml --
disableKinds = ['page','rss','section','sitemap','taxonomy','term']
-- layouts/home.html --
{{ $r := resources.Get "a.csv" }}
{{ $opts := dict "targetType" "map" "format" "csv" }}

title: Allow symlinks for mount source for the main project

judge.reasoning: Both patches make the same core change: skip the symlinked-mount-root rejection in NewRootMappingFs when rm.IsProject is set. That directly resolves the reported scenario (a project mount whose source directory is a symlink), and all three independent tests pass on both. The difference is completeness and test coverage. Patch B only lifts the check at mount-construction time; a project mount whose source is a single symlinked file still dies in statRoot's per-file symlink rejection, so the 'main project is trusted' rule B states in its comment is only half-implemented. Patch A carries the exemption through consistently: statRoot follows the symlink only when the mapping is a project single-file mount (root.fiSingleFile != nil, after rename/inclusion filtering has pinned filename to the mounted file), and componentFsDir keeps the corresponding entry under the same narrow condition. The extra code is small and guarded, so it adds little risk, and it closes an inconsistency a user hitting this issue would plausibly trip over next. Patch A's testscript is also stronger: it reproduces the issue's exact shape (an explicit 'content' mount plus a symlinked 'projectcontentroot' mounted at content/project-a, checked via site.GetPage), covers the symlinked-parent and single-file cases, and keeps the negative assertions that theme symlinked mounts, in-tree symlinked assets, and the symlinked page are still dropped, which guards against the exemption leaking to directory contents. Patch B's test is adequate but narrower, covering only asset directory mounts. No flaws found in B beyond the gap above; A is the more complete fix with better tests.

issue_md:
Hugo 0.166.0 introduced commit https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/commit/938c820626bd0a524dc1482cbe83b6c2e1171d20 (hugofs: Drop symlinked mount roots) that breaks a legit use-case of symlinks.

In my case, I mount a directory in my `hugo.yaml`:

```yaml
module:
  mounts:
    - source: "content"
      target: "content"
    # Mount content generated in another repository
    - source: "_build/includes/project-a"
      target: "content/project-a"
```

`_build/includes/project-a` itself can be a symlink to another local directory, e.g. `../../../project-a`, which allows quick local debugging. In production, a CI workflow may clone the Git repo of project-a to this destination which does not trigger the problem.

I am not familiar with the internals of hugofs and the security concept, but would appreciate if users could trust certain mounts, and therefore bypass the newly introduced hard drop of symlinks.

title: Support relative path calls in partials

judge.reasoning: Both patches implement the same core design: intercept names beginning with "./" or "../" in Include/IncludeCached, resolve them against the calling partial's directory taken from the current-template context, reject use outside partials and escapes above the partials root, and track a decoratorOwner so relative calls inside a `with partial` block resolve against the enclosing partial. Both pass eight of nine independent tests. The difference is the templates.Defer case. Patch A tries to support it by copying category and decoratorOwner into the deferred TemplInfo in addDeferredTemplate, but deferred templates are shared between owners with identical bodies, so the stored PathInfo belongs to whichever owner registered first. Two partials in different directories with textually identical defer blocks calling "./util.html" therefore both resolve to the first owner's sibling. The independent test TestBtJudgeRelativeInsideDeferIdenticalBodies confirms this: FAIL-ASSERT on A, PASS on B. Patch A's own defer test only has a single owner, so it does not catch the bug. Patch B instead resolves deferred templates via cur.Parent, the template that actually called templates.Defer, with an explicit comment about body sharing and a test with two identical defer blocks in different directories. This is a genuine correctness gap in A on a scenario the issue's "full path independent" goal implies, and A's change to addDeferredTemplate (setting category on deferred templates) also adds some risk of side effects elsewhere. B additionally covers the degenerate "./" case and flattens nested decoratorOwner chains at construction time; A's loop handles the chain equivalently. Tests are comparable in quality otherwise, with B also asserting that partialCached keys differ per directory. Docs are adequate in both. B wins on correctness.

issue_md:
Right now partial calls only supports path relative to `layout/partials` and `themes/<THEME>/layouts/partials/*<PARTIALNAME>` (taken from the documentation).

This is fine when we have few partials but can become a pain if we need to organize them in subdirectories.

What i propose is to add support for relative paths like in this example : 

```
{{ partial "./foo" ... }}
{{ partial "../bah" ... }}
```

## Why ?

Having this feature could be beneficial in a lot or ways : 
- it avoid us having to remember and write the full partial path when it's not needed (for example utility partials that are only called and only used by a on partial)
- It could allow us to reorganize partials way more easily, as relative paths would full path independent

## How to implement

If the path in a partial call starts with "./" or "../", it's a relative path. Otherwise it's an "absolute" path (relative to `layout/partials`).

I'm against adding the current directory of the current partial to the lookup search directly though, as theme and site authors currently assume this would call to the partial root directory. Perhaps we could add this to the future, if my proposal is adopted by the community.

+func (s *TemplateStore) ResolvePartialName(ctx context.Context, name string) (string, error) {
+	if !strings.HasPrefix(name, "./") && !strings.HasPrefix(name, "../") {
+		return name, nil
+	}
+	cur := tpl.Context.CurrentTemplate.Get(ctx)
+	if cur == nil {
+		return "", fmt.Errorf("relative partial path %q can only be used from within a partial", name)
+	}
+	ti := cur.CurrentTemplateInfoOps.(*TemplInfo)
+	for ti.decoratorOwner != nil {
+		ti = ti.decoratorOwner
+	}
+	if ti.category != CategoryPartial {
+		return "", fmt.Errorf("relative partial path %q can only be used from within a partial, called from %q", name, ti.Name())
+	}
+	dir := strings.TrimPrefix(strings.TrimPrefix(ti.PathInfo.Dir(), "/"+containerPartials), "/")
+	resolved := path.Join(dir, name)
+	if resolved == ".." || strings.HasPrefix(resolved, "../") {
+		return "", fmt.Errorf("relative partial path %q in %q resolves outside the partials directory", name, ti.Name())
+	}
+	return resolved, nil
